questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Classifying sexually transmitted infections by causative agent and curability from a table, and the correct and misused purposes of amniocentesis
questions.question: A health survey lists these sexually transmitted infections: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV infection. How many are caused by bacteria, how many by viruses, how many are not completely curable, and which statement about amniocentesis is correct?
options: A) Bacteria 4, viruses 3, incurable 1; amniocentesis is a contraceptive method

B) Bacteria 3 (gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis), viruses 4 (genital herpes, genital warts, hepatitis-B, HIV), the remaining one (trichomoniasis) protozoan; 3 are not completely curable (genital herpes, hepatitis-B, HIV); amniocentesis tests foetal cells in the amniotic fluid for genetic disorders, and its misuse for foetal sex determination is legally banned
C) Bacteria 2, viruses 5, incurable 5; amniocentesis is used only to find the sex of the foetus
D) Bacteria 3, viruses 4, incurable 0, since all STIs are fully curable with early treatment
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bacterial 3, viral 4, protozoan 1; 3 not completely curable; amniocentesis detects genetic disorders and its use for sex determination is banned.
Concept: Diseases or infections which are transmitted through sexual intercourse are collectively called sexually transmitted infections (STI) or venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI); gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV leading to AIDS are some of the common STIs. Some, like hepatitis-B and HIV, can also be transmitted by sharing of injection needles, surgical instruments, transfusion of blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus. Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, other diseases are completely curable if detected early and treated properly. Gonorrhoea (Neisseria), syphilis (Treponema) and chlamydiasis (Chlamydia) are bacterial; trichomoniasis is caused by the protozoan Trichomonas; herpes, warts (human papilloma virus), hepatitis-B and HIV are viral. Amniocentesis is a foetal sex determination test based on the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid surrounding the developing embryo; it is meant to detect genetic disorders, but because it has been misused to determine sex and kill normal female foetuses, there is a statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination.
Given: Eight infections.
Formula/Principle: Tally by causative agent; incurable = viral infections that persist (herpes, hepatitis-B, HIV).
Step 1: Bacterial: gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis = 3.
Step 2: Viral: herpes, warts, hepatitis-B, HIV = 4; protozoan: trichomoniasis = 1.
Step 3: Not completely curable: herpes, hepatitis-B, HIV = 3.
Why: Bacterial and protozoan STIs respond to drugs, while some viral infections persist in the body for life.
Why not the others: (A) Only three are bacterial; amniocentesis is not contraception. (C) Counts wrong; the test is meant for genetic disorders. (D) Three are not fully curable.
Key point: Herpes, hepatitis-B and HIV are not completely curable; amniocentesis for sex determination is banned.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the ABO blood groups as multiple alleles with co-dominance at the molecular level, predicting offspring of an AB × O cross, and explaining pleiotropy
questions.question: Which explanation of ABO blood groups and pleiotropy is correct?
options: A) ABO blood groups are controlled by two genes, so there are four genotypes and six phenotypes
B) The i allele produces a sugar that is masked by I^A
C) Pleiotropy means several genes together control one trait, as in skin colour

D) The gene I has three alleles, I^A, I^B and i; I^A and I^B code for slightly different enzymes that add different sugars to a polymer on the red cell surface, while i adds none, so I^A and I^B are both dominant over i but co-dominant with each other, giving six genotypes and four phenotypes; an AB × O cross gives only A (I^Ai) and B (I^Bi) children in a 1 : 1 ratio; pleiotropy is one gene affecting several phenotypes, as in phenylketonuria, where a mutation in the gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Three alleles, co-dominance of I^A and I^B, six genotypes and four phenotypes; AB × O gives A and B; PKU is pleiotropic.
Concept: ABO blood grouping provides a good example of multiple alleles. Blood groups are controlled by the gene I; the plasma membrane of the red blood cell has sugar polymers that protrude from its surface, and the kind of sugar is controlled by the gene. The gene I has three alleles, I^A, I^B and i; the alleles I^A and I^B produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele i does not produce any sugar. Because humans are diploid, each person possesses any two of the three I gene alleles; I^A and I^B are completely dominant over i — when I^A and i are present only I^A expresses — but when I^A and I^B are present together they both express their own types of sugars, because of co-dominance; hence red blood cells have both A and B types of sugars. Since there are three different alleles, there are six different combinations and therefore six genotypes of human ABO blood types, but only four phenotypes. Multiple alleles can be found only when population studies are made, because an individual carries only two. A single gene can exhibit multiple phenotypic expression; such a gene is called a pleiotropic gene; the underlying mechanism of pleiotropy in most cases is the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways which contribute towards different phenotypes; an example is phenylketonuria, a disease caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (single gene mutation), manifested through phenotypic expression characterised by mental retardation and a reduction in hair and skin pigmentation.
Given: Parents I^AI^B and ii.
Formula/Principle: Segregation of alleles; Punnett square.
Step 1: Gametes: I^A, I^B from AB; i from O.
Step 2: Offspring I^Ai (A) and I^Bi (B), 1 : 1.
Step 3: Genotypes: 3 homozygous + 3 heterozygous = 6; phenotypes A, B, AB, O = 4.
Why: Each functional allele makes its own enzyme product, so both show in the heterozygote, while the non-functional allele contributes nothing.
Why not the others: (A) One gene with three alleles; six genotypes, four phenotypes. (B) i adds no sugar. (C) That describes polygenic inheritance.
Key point: I^A = I^B > i; 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes; pleiotropy = one gene, many effects.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the length of DNA in a cell and the number of nucleosomes from base-pair counts, and explaining how negatively charged DNA is packed with histones and non-histone proteins
questions.question: The distance between two consecutive base pairs is 0.34 nm. A typical mammalian cell has 6.6 × 10⁹ bp of DNA, and E. coli has 4.6 × 10⁶ bp. One nucleosome contains about 200 bp. What are the DNA lengths, the approximate number of nucleosomes in the mammalian cell, and the correct packaging mechanism?
options: A) Mammalian DNA ≈ 2.2 m and E. coli DNA ≈ 1.6 mm; about 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes; the negatively charged DNA (phosphate groups) wraps around a positively charged histone octamer, rich in lysine and arginine, to form a nucleosome; nucleosomes look like 'beads-on-string', coil into chromatin fibres and are further packed with the help of non-histone chromosomal proteins; loosely packed, transcriptionally active chromatin is euchromatin and densely packed, inactive chromatin is heterochromatin
B) Mammalian DNA ≈ 22 m; 6.6 × 10⁹ nucleosomes; histones are negatively charged and repel DNA
C) Mammalian DNA ≈ 0.22 m; E. coli DNA ≈ 16 mm; 1.65 × 10⁷ nucleosomes; heterochromatin is transcriptionally active
D) Mammalian DNA ≈ 2.2 m; 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes; prokaryotic DNA is wrapped around histones in a membrane-bound nucleus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.2 m and about 1.6 mm; ≈ 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes; histone octamer, beads-on-string, NHC proteins, euchromatin and heterochromatin.
Concept: The distance between two consecutive base pairs is 0.34 nm (0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m); if the length of DNA double helix in a typical mammalian cell is calculated (simply by multiplying the total number of bp with the distance between two consecutive bp, that is, 6.6 × 10⁹ bp × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m/bp), it comes out to be approximately 2.2 metres — a length far greater than the dimension of a typical nucleus (approximately 10⁻⁶ m). In prokaryotes such as E. coli, though they do not have a defined nucleus, the DNA is not scattered throughout the cell; DNA (being negatively charged) is held with some proteins (that have positive charges) in a region termed the nucleoid. In eukaryotes there is a set of positively charged, basic proteins called histones; a protein acquires charge depending upon the abundance of amino acid residues with charged side chains, and histones are rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine, both of which carry positive charges in their side chains; histones are organised to form a unit of eight molecules called a histone octamer; the negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a structure called the nucleosome; a typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix. Nucleosomes constitute the repeating unit of a structure in the nucleus called chromatin; the nucleosomes in chromatin are seen as 'beads-on-string' under the electron microscope; the beads-on-string structure in chromatin is packaged to form chromatin fibres that are further coiled and condensed at metaphase to form chromosomes; the packaging of chromatin at higher level requires an additional set of proteins collectively referred to as non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins. In a typical nucleus, some regions of chromatin are loosely packed (and stain light) and are referred to as euchromatin; the chromatin that is more densely packed and stains dark is called heterochromatin; euchromatin is said to be transcriptionally active and heterochromatin inactive.
Given: 0.34 nm per bp; 6.6 × 10⁹ bp; 4.6 × 10⁶ bp; 200 bp per nucleosome.
Formula/Principle: Length = number of bp × 0.34 nm; nucleosomes ≈ total bp/200.
Step 1: 6.6 × 10⁹ × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.24 m ≈ 2.2 m.
Step 2: 4.6 × 10⁶ × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1.56 × 10⁻³ m ≈ 1.6 mm.
Step 3: 6.6 × 10⁹/200 = 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes.
Why: Opposite charges let DNA wind tightly around histones, achieving the huge compaction needed to fit metres of DNA into a micrometre-sized nucleus.
Why not the others: (B) Length off by ten; histones are positive. (C) Length and nucleosome count wrong; heterochromatin is inactive. (D) Prokaryotes lack histone-wrapped DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Key point: Length = bp × 0.34 nm; histone octamer + 200 bp = nucleosome.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of steps in curd formation by lactic acid bacteria, and the microbes used for bread, cheese and industrial acids, enzymes and bioactive molecules
questions.question: Which sequence and description is correct?
options: A) Milk is boiled to kill all bacteria, then left to curdle on its own because acids form spontaneously
B) Curd is formed by baker's yeast, which releases CO₂; Swiss cheese gets its holes from Lactobacillus

C) A small amount of curd added to fresh milk acts as an inoculum containing millions of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) → at suitable temperatures LAB multiply and produce acids → the acids coagulate and partially digest milk proteins, converting milk to curd, while LAB also increase vitamin B₁₂ and check disease-causing microbes in the stomach; similarly, baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments dough, the large holes in Swiss cheese come from CO₂ made by Propionibacterium sharmanii, and Roquefort cheese is ripened by fungi; industrially, Aspergillus niger gives citric acid, Acetobacter aceti acetic acid, Clostridium butylicum butyric acid and Lactobacillus lactic acid, while streptokinase (Streptococcus), cyclosporin A (Trichoderma polysporum) and statins (Monascus purpureus) are bioactive molecules
D) Statins are produced by Streptococcus and act as clot busters
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Inoculum → LAB multiply → acid coagulates and digests proteins → curd; correct microbe–product pairs.
Concept: Microorganisms such as Lactobacillus and others, commonly called lactic acid bacteria (LAB), grow in milk and convert it to curd; during growth, the LAB produce acids that coagulate and partially digest the milk proteins; a small amount of curd added to fresh milk as inoculum or starter contains millions of LAB, which at suitable temperatures multiply, thus converting milk to curd, which also improves its nutritional quality by increasing vitamin B₁₂; in our stomach too, the LAB play a very beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes. The dough used for making bread is fermented using baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). The large holes in 'Swiss cheese' are due to production of a large amount of CO₂ by a bacterium named Propionibacterium sharmanii; 'Roquefort cheese' is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it, which gives it a particular flavour. Microbes are also used to synthesise a number of products valuable to human beings: Aspergillus niger (a fungus) for citric acid, Acetobacter aceti (a bacterium) for acetic acid, Clostridium butylicum (a bacterium) for butyric acid and Lactobacillus (a bacterium) for lactic acid; yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is used for commercial production of ethanol; lipases are used in detergent formulations; bottled fruit juices are clearer because they are treated with pectinases and proteases. Streptokinase produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering is used as a 'clot buster'; cyclosporin A, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients, is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum; statins produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus have been commercialised as blood-cholesterol lowering agents, acting by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol.
Step 1: Inoculum supplies LAB.
Step 2: LAB multiply and make lactic acid.
Step 3: Acid coagulates and partly digests milk proteins.
Why: Acid lowers pH, which makes milk proteins coagulate, and the bacteria also add vitamin B₁₂ and suppress harmful microbes.
Why not the others: (A) Boiling kills LAB; an inoculum is required. (B) Curd is made by LAB; Swiss cheese holes come from Propionibacterium. (D) Statins come from Monascus and lower cholesterol; streptokinase is the clot buster.
Key point: Curd = LAB acid; citric (Aspergillus), acetic (Acetobacter), butyric (Clostridium), lactic (Lactobacillus).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing plasmids, the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium and retroviruses as cloning vectors, and the role of ori, selectable markers and unique cloning sites
questions.question: Which comparison of cloning vectors is correct?
options: A) A vector should have many recognition sites for the restriction enzyme used, so that it is cut into many pieces
B) The origin of replication only decides which antibiotic the host resists
C) Retroviruses cannot be used as vectors because they never enter animal cells

D) Every vector needs an origin of replication (ori), which starts replication and controls copy number, a selectable marker (such as genes for resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin) to identify transformants, and preferably a single recognition site for a restriction enzyme; bacterial plasmids are the commonest vectors; the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens naturally causes tumours in dicots but, once disarmed, delivers genes of interest into plants without causing tumours; retroviruses, which transform normal animal cells into cancerous ones, are disarmed and used to deliver genes into animal cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ori, selectable marker and single cloning site; plasmids for bacteria, disarmed Ti plasmid for plants, disarmed retroviruses for animal cells.
Concept: Bacterial plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA. Features required to facilitate cloning into a vector: (i) origin of replication (ori) — the sequence from where replication starts; any piece of DNA linked to it can be made to replicate within the host cells; this sequence is also responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA, so if one wants many copies of the target DNA it should be cloned in a vector whose origin supports high copy number; (ii) selectable marker — in addition to ori, the vector requires a selectable marker, which helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of transformants; normally, the genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli; (iii) cloning sites — in order to link the alien DNA, the vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes; presence of more than one recognition site within the vector will generate several fragments, which will complicate the gene cloning. Vectors for cloning genes in plants and animals: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as T-DNA to transform normal plant cells into a tumour and direct these tumour cells to produce the chemicals required by the pathogen; similarly, retroviruses in animals have the ability to transform normal cells into cancerous cells; the tumour-inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens has now been modified into a cloning vector which is no longer pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants; similarly, retroviruses have also been disarmed and are now used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.
Why: Each feature solves one problem — replication in the host, finding the cells that took up the vector, and opening the vector at one predictable place.
Why not the others: (A) Several sites give many fragments and complicate cloning. (B) ori controls replication and copy number; markers give resistance. (C) Retroviruses infect animal cells and, disarmed, deliver genes.
Key point: ori + selectable marker + unique site; disarmed Ti plasmid (plants), disarmed retrovirus (animals).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining how both partners benefit in mutualisms such as lichens, mycorrhizae, fig–wasp and orchid–bee, and why epiphytes, cattle egrets and barnacles are commensals
questions.question: Which explanation of mutualism and commensalism is correct?
options: A) Lichens are a parasitic association in which the fungus kills the alga

B) In a lichen the fungus provides shelter and absorbs mineral nutrients and water for the alga, which makes food photosynthetically; in mycorrhizae the fungus helps the plant absorb nutrients and the plant supplies energy-yielding carbohydrates; the fig is pollinated only by its partner wasp, which lays eggs in the fruit where the larvae feed on developing seeds; the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys has a petal resembling the female bee, so males 'pseudocopulate' and carry pollen; an orchid growing on a mango branch, cattle egrets catching insects stirred up by grazing cattle, and barnacles on a whale's back are commensalisms, as one partner benefits while the other is neither harmed nor helped
C) Commensalism benefits both partners equally
D) The cattle egret harms cattle by feeding on them, so it is parasitism
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Lichen, mycorrhiza, fig–wasp and Ophrys–bee mutualisms; epiphytic orchid, cattle egret and barnacles as commensals.
Concept: Mutualism is an interaction that confers benefits on both the interacting species. Lichens represent an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria; similarly, the mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and the roots of higher plants; the fungal symbionts help the plant in the absorption of essential nutrients from the soil while the plant in turn provides the fungi with energy-yielding carbohydrates. The most spectacular and evolutionarily fascinating examples of mutualism are found in plant–animal relationships; in many species of fig trees, there is a tight one-to-one relationship with the pollinator species of wasp; a given fig species can be pollinated only by its 'partner' wasp species and no other species; the female wasp uses the fruit not only as an oviposition (egg-laying) site but uses the developing seeds within the fruit for nourishing its larvae; the wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites; in return for the favour of pollination, the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds as food for the developing wasp larvae. The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs 'sexual deceit' to get pollination done by a species of bee; one petal of its flower bears an uncanny resemblance to the female of the bee in size, colour and markings; the male bee is attracted to what it perceives as a female, 'pseudocopulates' with the flower, and during that process is dusted with pollen from the flower; when this same bee 'pseudocopulates' with another flower, it transfers pollen to it and thus pollinates the flower. Commensalism is the interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited; an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch, and barnacles growing on the back of a whale benefit while neither the mango tree nor the whale derives any apparent benefit; the cattle egret and grazing cattle in close association is a classic example: the egrets always forage close to where the cattle are grazing because the cattle, as they move, stir up and flush out insects from the vegetation that otherwise might be difficult for the egrets to find and catch; another example is the sea anemone with stinging tentacles and the clown fish that lives among them — the fish gets protection from predators which stay away from the stinging tentacles, while the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit.
Why: In mutualism each partner supplies something the other cannot get easily, and in tight mutualisms the partners coevolve.
Why not the others: (A) Lichens are mutualistic. (C) In commensalism only one partner benefits. (D) Egrets eat insects flushed out by cattle; cattle are unharmed.
Key point: Mutualism (+/+): lichen, mycorrhiza, fig–wasp, Ophrys–bee; commensalism (+/0): epiphyte, egret, barnacle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the 10 per cent law of energy transfer along a grazing food chain and explaining why energy flow is unidirectional and food chains are short
questions.question: Producers in a grassland trap 20 000 kJ of energy in a season. Using the 10 per cent law, how much energy reaches the secondary and the tertiary consumers, and which statement about energy flow is correct?
options: A) Secondary consumers get 200 kJ and tertiary consumers 20 kJ; plants capture only 2–10 per cent of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR); at each transfer most energy is lost as heat in respiration, so energy flows in one direction from the sun to producers to consumers and is not recycled, which limits food chains to a few trophic levels; the grazing food chain begins with producers, while the detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter and is the major conduit of energy flow in terrestrial ecosystems
B) Secondary consumers get 2000 kJ and tertiary 1000 kJ, since half is passed on at each step
C) Energy is recycled from decomposers back to producers, so food chains can be very long
D) Tertiary consumers get 2 kJ; producers capture all the sunlight that falls on them
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 200 kJ and 20 kJ; unidirectional flow with large losses as heat.
Concept: Except for the deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystem, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on earth; of the incident solar radiation, less than 50 per cent is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR); plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR, and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world. Ecosystems are not exempt from the second law of thermodynamics; they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise the molecules they require, to counteract the universal tendency toward increasing disorderliness; there is unidirectional flow of energy from the sun to producers and then to consumers. Producers (green plants) are eaten by herbivores (primary consumers), which are eaten by carnivores (secondary consumers), and so on; the food chain starting from the producers is the grazing food chain (GFC); the detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter and is made up of decomposers which are heterotrophic organisms, mainly fungi and bacteria; in an aquatic ecosystem GFC is the major conduit for energy flow, while in a terrestrial ecosystem a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain than through the GFC. The amount of energy decreases at successive trophic levels; only 10 per cent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level (the 10 per cent law), the rest being used in respiration and lost as heat.
Given: Energy at producers = 20 000 kJ.
Formula/Principle: Energy at level n+1 = 0.10 × energy at level n.
Step 1: Primary consumers: 0.10 × 20 000 = 2000 kJ.
Step 2: Secondary consumers: 0.10 × 2000 = 200 kJ.
Step 3: Tertiary consumers: 0.10 × 200 = 20 kJ.
Why: Each level spends most of the energy it receives on its own life processes, releasing it as heat that cannot be passed on.
Why not the others: (B) Transfer is about 10 per cent, not 50 per cent. (C) Energy is not recycled; nutrients are. (D) Tertiary level gets 20 kJ; plants capture only a small part of PAR.
Key point: 10 per cent law; energy flows one way and is lost as heat.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting observations on biodiversity hotspots, protected areas and sacred groves as forms of in situ conservation
questions.question: (i) A region covering a small fraction of the earth's land area holds a very large number of species found nowhere else and has lost much of its habitat. (ii) A tribal community has protected a forest patch for generations for religious reasons, and rare species survive only there. (iii) A government declares an area where the whole ecosystem, with its wildlife, is protected. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) All three are examples of ex situ conservation because people manage the species
B) (i) is a botanical garden, (ii) a zoo and (iii) a seed bank

C) (i) is a biodiversity hotspot — a region of very high species richness and endemism under threat; 34 hotspots together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area and three of them (Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya) cover India's exceptionally rich biodiversity regions; (ii) is a sacred grove, found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh, where all trees and wildlife are venerated and protected and endangered species survive; (iii) is a protected area such as a national park, wildlife sanctuary or biosphere reserve; all three conserve species in their natural habitat (in situ)
D) Sacred groves are areas cleared by tribals for agriculture
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (i) hotspot, (ii) sacred grove, (iii) protected area — all in situ conservation.
Concept: When we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all levels is protected — this approach is in situ (on site) conservation. Faced with the conflict between development and conservation, many nations find it unrealistic to protect all their biological wealth, and conservationists identified for maximum protection certain 'biodiversity hotspots' — regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism (that is, species confined to that region and not found anywhere else); initially 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified, but subsequently nine more were added, bringing the total to 34; these hotspots are also regions of accelerated habitat loss; three of these hotspots — Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya — cover our country's exceptionally high biodiversity regions; although all the biodiversity hotspots put together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area, the number of species they collectively harbour is extremely high, and strict protection of these hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent. In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries. India has also a history of religious and cultural traditions that emphasised protection of nature; in many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside, and all the trees and wildlife within were venerated and given total protection; such sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh; in Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants. Ex situ (off site) conservation, in contrast, takes threatened animals and plants out of their natural habitat into special settings such as zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks and seed banks.
Why: Each case protects species where they naturally live, along with the ecosystem that sustains them.
Why not the others: (A) Species remain in their natural habitat, so this is in situ. (B) Those are ex situ methods. (D) Sacred groves are protected, not cleared.
Key point: Hotspots, protected areas and sacred groves are in situ conservation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the distinguishing features of Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes and Deuteromycetes in terms of mycelium, spores and the steps of sexual reproduction
questions.question: Which explanation of the classes of fungi is correct?
options: A) In all fungi karyogamy follows plasmogamy immediately, so a dikaryon never forms

B) Phycomycetes (e.g. Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo) have aseptate, coenocytic mycelium and reproduce asexually by zoospores or aplanospores, sexually forming zygospores; Ascomycetes (sac fungi, e.g. Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, yeast) have septate mycelium, exogenous conidia and endogenous ascospores in asci; Basidiomycetes (mushrooms, bracket fungi, smuts, rusts) have septate mycelium, generally lack asexual spores and sex organs, show plasmogamy by fusion of vegetative cells, and produce four basidiospores exogenously on a basidium after karyogamy and meiosis; Deuteromycetes are called imperfect fungi because only their asexual (conidial) phase is known, and when the sexual form is discovered they are moved to their proper class
C) Basidiospores are formed inside asci, while ascospores are formed on basidia
D) Deuteromycetes are called imperfect because they lack hyphae
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Correct features of the four classes, including the reason Deuteromycetes are 'imperfect'.
Concept: Fungi reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation, fission and budding; asexually by spores called conidia, sporangiospores or zoospores; and sexually by oospores, ascospores and basidiospores. The sexual cycle involves three steps: (i) fusion of protoplasms between two motile or non-motile gametes, called plasmogamy; (ii) fusion of two nuclei, called karyogamy; (iii) meiosis in the zygote resulting in haploid spores. In some fungi the fusion of two haploid cells immediately results in diploid cells; in other fungi (ascomycetes and basidiomycetes), an intervening dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell) occurs; such a condition is called a dikaryon and the phase is called the dikaryophase. Phycomycetes are found in aquatic habitats and on decaying wood in moist and damp places or as obligate parasites on plants; the mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic; asexual reproduction takes place by zoospores (motile) or by aplanospores (non-motile), endogenously produced in sporangium; a zygospore is formed by fusion of two gametes. Ascomycetes (sac-fungi) are mostly multicellular, e.g. Penicillium, or rarely unicellular, e.g. yeast; mycelium is branched and septate; the asexual spores are conidia produced exogenously on special mycelium called conidiophores; sexual spores are called ascospores, produced endogenously in sac-like asci, arranged inside fruiting bodies called ascocarps; some examples are Aspergillus, Claviceps and Neurospora. Basidiomycetes (mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs, smuts and rusts) have branched septate mycelium; asexual spores are generally not found, but vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common; sex organs are absent, but plasmogamy is brought about by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains or genotypes; the resultant structure is dikaryotic, which ultimately gives rise to the basidium, where karyogamy and meiosis take place to produce four basidiospores, produced exogenously on the basidium. Deuteromycetes are commonly known as imperfect fungi because only the asexual or vegetative phases of these fungi are known; when the sexual forms of these fungi were discovered they were moved into classes they rightly belong to; they reproduce only by asexual spores known as conidia; the mycelium is septate and branched (e.g. Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma).
Why: Classes are separated mainly by whether hyphae are septate and by how and where sexual spores form, so a fungus without a known sexual stage cannot be placed.
Why not the others: (A) Ascomycetes and basidiomycetes have a dikaryophase. (C) Spore positions swapped. (D) Deuteromycetes have septate hyphae; they lack only a known sexual stage.
Key point: Zygospore (Phycomycetes), ascospore in ascus (Ascomycetes), basidiospore on basidium (Basidiomycetes), sexual stage unknown (Deuteromycetes).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a comparison table of pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella to identify the three classes of algae
questions.question:
Three algae X, Y and Z are compared:

Alga | Main pigments | Stored food | Cell wall | Flagella
X | chlorophyll a, b | starch | cellulose | 2–8, equal, apical
Y | chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin | mannitol, laminarin | cellulose and algin | 2, unequal, lateral
Z | chlorophyll a, d, phycoerythrin | floridean starch | cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters | absent

Which identification is correct?
options: A) X Rhodophyceae, Y Chlorophyceae, Z Phaeophyceae
B) X Phaeophyceae (e.g. Laminaria), Y Rhodophyceae (e.g. Polysiphonia), Z Chlorophyceae (e.g. Ulothrix)
C) X Chlorophyceae, Y Rhodophyceae, Z Phaeophyceae; all three classes have motile flagellated stages

D) X Chlorophyceae (green algae, e.g. Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara), Y Phaeophyceae (brown algae, e.g. Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus), Z Rhodophyceae (red algae, e.g. Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium); red algae owe their colour to r-phycoerythrin and can live at great depths where little light penetrates
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) X green (Chlorophyceae), Y brown (Phaeophyceae), Z red (Rhodophyceae).
Concept: Algae are divided into three main classes: Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae. Chlorophyceae (green algae) have chlorophyll a and b localised in definite chloroplasts; most members have one or more storage bodies called pyrenoids containing protein besides starch; they have a rigid cell wall made of an inner layer of cellulose and an outer layer of pectose; flagella are 2–8, equal and apical. Phaeophyceae (brown algae) are found primarily in marine habitats; they possess chlorophyll a, c, carotenoids and xanthophylls, and vary in colour from olive green to various shades of brown depending upon the amount of the xanthophyll pigment fucoxanthin present; food is stored as complex carbohydrates in the form of laminarin or mannitol; the vegetative cells have a cellulosic wall usually covered on the outside by a gelatinous coating of algin; zoospores are pear-shaped and bear two unequal laterally attached flagella. Rhodophyceae (red algae) are so called because of the predominance of the red pigment r-phycoerythrin in their body; the majority are marine, with greater concentrations found in the warmer areas; they occur in both well-lighted regions close to the surface of water and also at great depths in oceans where relatively little light penetrates; the food is stored as floridean starch, which is very similar to amylopectin and glycogen in structure; the cell wall contains cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters; flagella are absent.
Why: Pigment composition, stored food and flagellar arrangement are diagnostic for each class.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) Classes mismatched with their pigments. (C) Y and Z swapped; red algae lack flagella.
Key point: Green (a, b; starch), brown (a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin/mannitol), red (a, d, phycoerythrin; floridean starch, no flagella).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying knowledge of root, stem and leaf modifications to predict the adaptations of plants in swampy, arid and climbing conditions
questions.question: (i) A tree grows in a mangrove swamp where the soil is waterlogged and poor in oxygen. (ii) A plant grows in a desert with very little water. (iii) A weak-stemmed plant needs support to climb. Which prediction of modifications is correct?
options: A) (i) Roots grow vertically upwards above the ground as pneumatophores (as in Rhizophora) to get oxygen for respiration; (ii) the stem becomes a flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) green photosynthetic organ, while leaves are reduced to spines to cut water loss; (iii) tendrils develop — from axillary buds as stem tendrils in cucumber, pumpkin and grapevine, or from leaflets in pea; in addition, thorns of Citrus and Bougainvillea are modified axillary buds that protect from browsing animals
B) (i) Roots become fleshy to store food, as in carrot; (ii) leaves become broad and thin
C) (iii) Tendrils always arise from roots, and thorns are modified leaves
D) (ii) The plant develops prop roots like the banyan tree to absorb more water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pneumatophores, phylloclade with leaf spines, and stem or leaf tendrils.
Concept: Roots in some plants change their shape and structure and become modified to perform functions other than absorption and conduction of water and minerals; they are modified for support, storage of food and respiration; tap roots of carrot and turnip and adventitious roots of sweet potato get swollen and store food; hanging structures that support a banyan tree are called prop roots; similarly, the stems of maize and sugarcane have supporting roots coming out of the lower nodes of the stem, called stilt roots; in some plants such as Rhizophora growing in swampy areas, many roots come out of the ground and grow vertically upwards; such roots, called pneumatophores, help to get oxygen for respiration. The stem may not always be typically like what it is expected to be; it is modified to perform different functions; stem tendrils which develop from axillary buds are slender and spirally coiled and help plants to climb, such as in gourds (cucumber, pumpkins, watermelon) and grapevines; axillary buds of stems may also get modified into woody, straight and pointed thorns; thorns are found in many plants such as Citrus and Bougainvillea, and they protect plants from browsing animals; some plants of arid regions modify their stems into flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) structures; they contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. Leaves are often modified to perform functions other than photosynthesis; they are converted into tendrils for climbing as in peas or into spines for defence as in cacti.
Why: Each modification solves the problem the environment poses — oxygen for roots, water saving, or support for climbing.
Why not the others: (B) Storage roots and broad leaves do not suit swamps or deserts. (C) Tendrils come from stems or leaves; thorns are modified axillary buds. (D) Prop roots support large trees; they are not a desert adaptation.
Key point: Pneumatophores (swamps), phylloclades and spines (deserts), tendrils (climbers).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting stained transverse sections of two roots to identify dicot and monocot roots from xylem bundle number, pith and secondary growth
questions.question: A student stains transverse sections of two young roots with safranin. Root P shows 4 xylem bundles alternating with phloem, a small or no pith, and, in an older piece, a ring of cambium. Root Q shows more than 6 xylem bundles, a large well-developed pith and no secondary growth. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Both are monocot roots because both have radial bundles
B) P is a monocot root and Q a dicot root, since monocots have fewer bundles

C) P is a dicot root (e.g. bean, with 2–4 xylem bundles — diarch to tetrarch) and Q a monocot root (e.g. maize, usually more than six bundles — polyarch); in both, the endodermis has Casparian strips and the pericycle initiates lateral roots; in the dicot root, the conjunctive tissue between xylem and phloem and part of the pericycle form a cambium that produces secondary tissues, while monocot roots have a large pith and do not undergo secondary growth
D) Lateral roots arise from the epidermis in both roots
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P dicot (2–4 bundles, cambium later), Q monocot (polyarch, large pith, no secondary growth).
Concept: In the transverse section of a typical dicot root (e.g. sunflower or bean), the outermost layer is the epiblema, many of whose cells protrude as unicellular root hairs; the cortex consists of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma cells with intercellular spaces; the innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis, a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces, whose tangential and radial walls have a deposition of water-impermeable, waxy suberin as Casparian strips; next to the endodermis lie a few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells referred to as pericycle; initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during secondary growth takes place in these cells; the pith is small or inconspicuous; the parenchymatous cells which lie between the xylem and the phloem are called conjunctive tissue; there are usually two to four xylem and phloem patches; later, a cambium ring develops between the xylem and phloem; all tissues on the inner side of the endodermis such as pericycle, vascular bundles and pith constitute the stele. The anatomy of the monocot root is similar to the dicot root in many respects; it has epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles and pith; as compared to the dicot root which has fewer xylem bundles, there are usually more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles in the monocot root; pith is large and well developed; monocotyledonous roots do not undergo any secondary growth.
Why: Bundle number, pith size and the presence of cambium are the features that distinguish the two root types.
Why not the others: (A) Both have radial bundles, but bundle number and secondary growth show P is a dicot. (B) Monocot roots have more bundles. (D) Lateral roots arise from the pericycle.
Key point: Dicot root 2–4 bundles, cambium; monocot root polyarch, large pith, no secondary growth.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the circulatory system and nervous system of the frog, including the heart chambers, portal systems and divisions of the brain
questions.question: Which explanation of the frog's circulatory and nervous systems is correct?
options: A) Frogs have a four-chambered heart and open circulation like insects
B) Frogs have no portal systems; all venous blood goes straight to the heart
C) The frog brain has no forebrain; the cerebral hemispheres lie in the hindbrain

D) Frogs have a closed vascular system with a three-chambered heart (two atria and one ventricle) covered by pericardium; a sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives blood from the venae cavae, and the ventricle opens into a conus arteriosus on the ventral side of the heart; special venous connections — the hepatic portal system between liver and intestine and the renal portal system between kidney and lower body parts — are present; the brain is divided into forebrain (olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres and diencephalon), midbrain (a pair of optic lobes) and hindbrain (cerebellum and medulla oblongata), with ten pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Closed system, three-chambered heart with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus, hepatic and renal portal systems; brain divisions and ten pairs of cranial nerves.
Concept: The vascular system of the frog is well developed and closed; frogs have a lymphatic system also; the blood vascular system involves the heart, blood vessels and blood, and the lymphatic system consists of lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes; the heart is a muscular structure situated in the upper part of the body cavity; it has three chambers, two atria and one ventricle, and is covered by a membrane called pericardium; a triangular structure called sinus venosus joins the right atrium; it receives blood through the major veins called vena cava; the ventricle opens into a sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side of the heart; the blood from the heart is carried to all parts of the body by the arteries (arterial system), and the veins collect blood from different parts of the body to the heart and form the venous system; special venous connections between the liver and intestine as well as the kidney and lower parts of the body are present in frogs; the former is called the hepatic portal system and the latter the renal portal system. The blood is composed of plasma and cells; the blood cells are RBC (red blood cells) or erythrocytes, WBC (white blood cells) or leucocytes and platelets; RBCs are nucleated and contain the red pigment haemoglobin. The system for control and coordination is highly evolved in the frog; it includes both neural and endocrine systems; the nervous system is organised into a central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), a peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves) and an autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic); there are ten pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain; the brain is enclosed in a bony structure called the brain box (cranium); the brain is divided into fore-brain, mid-brain and hind-brain; the forebrain includes olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres and an unpaired diencephalon; the midbrain is characterised by a pair of optic lobes; the hindbrain consists of cerebellum and medulla oblongata, and the medulla oblongata passes out through the foramen magnum and continues into the spinal cord, which is enclosed in the vertebral column.
Why: The portal systems route blood through the liver and kidneys before it returns to the heart, and each brain division contains lobes for specific senses and control.
Why not the others: (A) Frogs have a three-chambered heart and closed circulation. (B) Hepatic and renal portal systems are present. (C) Cerebral hemispheres belong to the forebrain.
Key point: Frog: 3-chambered heart, sinus venosus, conus arteriosus; hepatic and renal portal systems; 10 pairs of cranial nerves.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the structure, composition and functions of the cell membrane (fluid mosaic model) with those of the plant cell wall
questions.question: Which comparison of the cell membrane and the cell wall is correct?
options: A) The cell membrane, described by the fluid mosaic model of Singer and Nicolson (1972), is a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer in which proteins move laterally; the erythrocyte membrane has about 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipid; its fluidity is important for cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division, and it transports molecules passively (by diffusion and osmosis) and actively (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump using ATP); the cell wall is a non-living rigid layer — of cellulose, galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate in algae, and of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins in plants — while the middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, holds neighbouring cells together and plasmodesmata connect their cytoplasm
B) The cell membrane is rigid and made only of cellulose, while the cell wall is a living lipid bilayer
C) In the fluid mosaic model proteins are fixed and cannot move
D) The middle lamella is made of chitin and is found only in animal cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Fluid mosaic membrane with its composition and functions; non-living cell wall, middle lamella and plasmodesmata.
Concept: Detailed structure of the membrane was studied only after the advent of the electron microscope in the 1950s; chemical studies on the cell membrane, especially in human red blood cells (RBCs), enabled scientists to deduce the possible structure of the plasma membrane; these studies showed that the cell membrane is composed of lipids that are arranged in a bilayer; the lipids are arranged within the membrane with the polar head towards the outer sides and the hydrophobic tails towards the inner part; later, biochemical investigation clearly revealed that cell membranes also possess protein and carbohydrate; the ratio of protein and lipid varies considerably in different cell types; in human beings, the membrane of the erythrocyte has approximately 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipids. An improved model of the structure of the cell membrane was proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972), widely accepted as the fluid mosaic model; according to this, the quasi-fluid nature of lipid enables lateral movement of proteins within the overall bilayer; this ability to move within the membrane is measured as its fluidity; the fluid nature of the membrane is also important from the point of view of functions like cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis, cell division, etc. One of the most important functions of the plasma membrane is the transport of molecules across it; the membrane is selectively permeable; many molecules can move briefly across the membrane without any requirement of energy, which is called passive transport; neutral solutes may move by simple diffusion along the concentration gradient; water may also move by osmosis; a few ions or molecules are transported across the membrane against their concentration gradient, which is an energy-dependent process in which ATP is utilised and is called active transport, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. The cell wall is a non-living rigid structure which forms an outer covering for the plasma membrane of fungi and plants; algae have cell walls made of cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like calcium carbonate, while in other plants it consists of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins; the cell wall of a young plant cell, the primary wall, is capable of growth, which gradually diminishes as the cell matures and the secondary wall is formed on the inner (towards membrane) side of the cell; the middle lamella is a layer mainly of calcium pectate which holds or glues the different neighbouring cells together; the cell wall and middle lamellae may be traversed by plasmodesmata which connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.
Why: The membrane must be flexible and selective to control exchange, while the wall must be rigid to give shape and protection.
Why not the others: (B) Descriptions reversed. (C) Proteins move laterally in the fluid bilayer. (D) The middle lamella is calcium pectate and occurs in plants.
Key point: Fluid mosaic membrane (lipid bilayer + mobile proteins); rigid non-living wall with middle lamella and plasmodesmata.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of stages of meiosis II after interkinesis, how it differs from meiosis I, and the significance of meiosis
questions.question: Which sequence and description of meiosis II and the significance of meiosis is correct?
options: A) Interkinesis includes DNA replication → prophase II → metaphase II → anaphase II → telophase II, and meiosis II halves the chromosome number

B) Interkinesis, a short stage without DNA replication → prophase II, in which the nuclear membrane disappears and chromosomes become compact again → metaphase II, in which chromosomes align at the equator and microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of sister chromatids → anaphase II, in which the centromere of each chromosome splits, allowing sister chromatids to move to opposite poles → telophase II, in which the two groups of chromosomes get enclosed by a nuclear envelope, followed by cytokinesis, giving a tetrad of four haploid cells; meiosis conserves the specific chromosome number of each species across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, and it increases genetic variability, which is important for evolution
C) In anaphase II homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay together
D) Meiosis II reduces variation, since it is identical to mitosis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Interkinesis (no replication) → prophase II → metaphase II → anaphase II (centromeres split) → telophase II; meiosis conserves chromosome number and creates variation.
Concept: The stage between the two meiotic divisions is called interkinesis and is generally short-lived; there is no replication of DNA during interkinesis; interkinesis is followed by prophase II, a much simpler prophase than prophase I. Meiosis II is initiated immediately after cytokinesis, usually before the chromosomes have fully elongated; in contrast to meiosis I, meiosis II resembles a normal mitosis. Prophase II: the nuclear membrane disappears by the end of prophase II and the chromosomes again become compact. Metaphase II: at this stage the chromosomes align at the equator and the microtubules from opposite poles of the spindle get attached to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. Anaphase II: it begins with the simultaneous splitting of the centromere of each chromosome (which was holding the sister chromatids together), allowing them to move toward opposite poles of the cell by shortening of microtubules attached to kinetochores. Telophase II: meiosis ends with telophase II, in which the two groups of chromosomes once again get enclosed by a nuclear envelope; cytokinesis follows, resulting in the formation of a tetrad of cells, i.e. four haploid daughter cells. Significance of meiosis: meiosis is the mechanism by which conservation of the specific chromosome number of each species is achieved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, even though the process, per se, paradoxically, results in reduction of chromosome number by half; it also increases the genetic variability in the population of organisms from one generation to the next; variations are very important for the process of evolution.
Step 1: Interkinesis without DNA replication.
Step 2: Prophase II and metaphase II (chromosomes at equator).
Step 3: Anaphase II (centromere splits) and telophase II → four haploid cells.
Why: Meiosis I separates homologues (reducing chromosome number), and meiosis II separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis.
Why not the others: (A) No DNA replication in interkinesis; reduction occurs in meiosis I. (C) Homologues separate in anaphase I. (D) Meiosis as a whole increases variation.
Key point: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids; meiosis keeps chromosome number constant and creates variation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a comparison table of C3 and C4 plants to identify the correct entries for primary CO₂ acceptor, first product, leaf anatomy, location of RuBisCO and photorespiration
questions.question:
A student fills in a table comparing C3 and C4 plants:

Feature | C3 plant | C4 plant
1. Primary CO₂ acceptor | RuBP (5C) | PEP (3C)
2. First stable product | PGA (3C) | OAA (4C)
3. Leaf anatomy | Kranz anatomy | no Kranz anatomy
4. Calvin cycle in | mesophyll cells | bundle sheath cells
5. Photorespiration | present | absent or negligible
6. Productivity at high temperature and light | higher | lower

How many rows are correct?
options: A) All 6
B) 3 (rows 1, 2 and 5)

C) 4 (rows 1, 2, 4 and 5); row 3 is reversed (C4 plants such as maize and sorghum have Kranz anatomy, with large bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles), and row 6 is reversed (C4 plants tolerate higher temperatures, respond to high light intensities and have greater productivity, because the C4 pathway raises CO₂ concentration around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath, which prevents its oxygenase activity)
D) 5 (all except row 6)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Four rows correct; rows 3 and 6 are reversed.
Concept: In C3 plants the primary acceptor of CO₂ is RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate, a 5-carbon ketose sugar), and the first stable product is the 3-carbon compound 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA). Plants that are adapted to dry tropical regions have the C4 pathway; though these plants have the C4 oxaloacetic acid (OAA) as the first CO₂ fixation product, they use the C3 pathway or the Calvin cycle as the main biosynthetic pathway. C4 plants are special: they have a special type of leaf anatomy, they tolerate higher temperatures, they show a response to high light intensities, they lack a process called photorespiration and they have greater productivity of biomass. The particularly large cells around the vascular bundles of the C4 pathway plants are called bundle sheath cells, and the leaves which have such anatomy are said to have 'Kranz' anatomy ('Kranz' means 'wreath'). In C4 plants, the primary CO₂ acceptor is the 3-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), present in the mesophyll cells, and the enzyme responsible is PEP carboxylase or PEPcase; mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO; the C4 acid OAA is formed in the mesophyll cells; it then forms other 4-carbon compounds like malic acid or aspartic acid, which are transported to the bundle sheath cells; in the bundle sheath cells these C4 acids are broken down to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule; the 3-carbon molecule is transported back to the mesophyll where it is converted to PEP again, completing the cycle; the CO₂ released in the bundle sheath cells enters the C3 or Calvin pathway, common to all plants; the bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase. RuBisCO can bind both CO₂ and O₂; in C3 plants some O₂ binds with RuBisCO, and hence CO₂ fixation is decreased (photorespiration), which wastes energy; in C4 plants photorespiration does not occur because they have a mechanism that increases the concentration of CO₂ at the enzyme site.
Given: Six rows.
Formula/Principle: Compare each entry with the known features of C3 and C4 plants.
Step 1: Rows 1 and 2 correct (RuBP/PGA vs PEP/OAA).
Step 2: Row 4 correct (Calvin cycle in bundle sheath of C4); row 5 correct.
Step 3: Row 3 (Kranz anatomy belongs to C4) and row 6 (C4 more productive) reversed ⇒ 4 correct.
Why: Concentrating CO₂ in bundle sheath cells lets C4 plants avoid photorespiration, which pays off most at high temperature and light.
Why not the others: (A) Two rows are reversed. (B) Row 4 is also correct. (D) Row 3 is also wrong.
Key point: C4: PEP → OAA in mesophyll, Calvin cycle in bundle sheath (Kranz), no photorespiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using the respiratory balance sheet to compare ATP yield and glucose use in aerobic respiration and alcoholic fermentation, and the assumptions behind the 38 ATP figure
questions.question: A yeast culture is grown with the same ATP requirement first under aerobic and then under anaerobic conditions. Using the theoretical balance sheet (38 ATP per glucose aerobically, 2 ATP per glucose in fermentation), how many times more glucose is consumed anaerobically, and which statement about the balance sheet is correct?
options: A) The same amount, since ATP yield does not depend on oxygen
B) 2 times; the 38 ATP figure is measured exactly in every living cell
C) 36 times; NADH made in glycolysis gives ATP in fermentation too

D) 19 times (38/2); the net gain of 38 ATP per glucose rests on assumptions — a sequential, orderly pathway with one substrate forming the next, glycolysis, the TCA cycle and the ETS working one after another, NADH from glycolysis transferred into mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation, no intermediates diverted to make other compounds, and only glucose being respired — which do not hold strictly in a living system, so the figure is a theoretical maximum
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 19 times more glucose; 38 ATP is a theoretical figure based on simplifying assumptions.
Concept: It is possible to make calculations of the net gain of ATP for every glucose molecule oxidised; but in reality this can remain only a theoretical exercise; these calculations can be made only on certain assumptions: there is a sequential, orderly pathway functioning, with one substrate forming the next and with glycolysis, the TCA cycle and ETS pathway following one after another; the NADH synthesised in glycolysis is transferred into the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation; none of the intermediates in the pathway are utilised to synthesise any other compound; only glucose is being respired — no other alternative substrates are entering the pathway at any of the intermediary stages. But these kinds of assumptions are not really valid in a living system; all pathways work simultaneously and do not take place one after another; substrates enter the pathways and are withdrawn from them as and when necessary; ATP is utilised as and when needed; enzymatic rates are controlled by multiple means; yet it is useful to do this exercise to appreciate the beauty and efficiency of the living system in extraction and storage of energy; hence, there can be a net gain of 38 ATP molecules during aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose. In fermentation, say by yeast, the incomplete oxidation of glucose is achieved under anaerobic conditions by sets of reactions where pyruvic acid is converted to CO₂ and ethanol; there is a net gain of only two molecules of ATP for each molecule of glucose degraded to pyruvic acid (in alcoholic fermentation), and NADH is oxidised to NAD⁺ rather slowly, without making ATP.
Given: Aerobic 38 ATP/glucose; anaerobic 2 ATP/glucose; equal ATP need.
Formula/Principle: Glucose needed ∝ ATP required/ATP per glucose.
Step 1: Let the requirement be 38 ATP.
Step 2: Aerobic: 1 glucose; anaerobic: 38/2 = 19 glucose.
Step 3: Ratio = 19.
Why: Fermentation stops at pyruvate breakdown, leaving most of the energy of glucose in ethanol, so far more glucose must be used for the same ATP.
Why not the others: (A) Oxygen allows the TCA cycle and ETS, raising the yield greatly. (B) The ratio is 19, and 38 is theoretical. (C) In fermentation NADH is reoxidised without ATP formation.
Key point: 38 vs 2 ATP ⇒ 19 times more glucose anaerobically; 38 ATP is a theoretical maximum.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting a starch–iodine experiment with saliva at different conditions, and the roles of salivary amylase, pepsin, bile and enterokinase along the alimentary canal
questions.question: Three test tubes contain starch solution with iodine (blue-black). Tube 1 gets fresh saliva at 37 °C; tube 2 gets boiled saliva at 37 °C; tube 3 gets fresh saliva with excess acid (pH about 2). After 20 min, only tube 1 has lost the blue-black colour. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Saliva contains pepsin, which digests starch best in acid

B) Salivary amylase digests starch into maltose, so tube 1 loses the blue colour; boiling denatures the enzyme (tube 2), and very low pH inactivates it (tube 3), since salivary amylase works best near pH 6.8 and hydrolyses about 30 per cent of starch in the mouth; in the stomach, pepsin, secreted as inactive pepsinogen and activated by HCl, digests proteins; bile, from the liver, contains no enzymes but emulsifies fats; and trypsinogen from the pancreas is activated to trypsin by enterokinase secreted by the intestinal mucosa
C) Bile from saliva emulsifies starch in tube 1
D) Starch digestion needs no enzyme, so all tubes should lose colour equally
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Amylase digests starch; boiling and very low pH inactivate it; roles of pepsin, bile and enterokinase.
Concept: The buccal cavity performs two major functions, mastication of food and facilitation of swallowing; the saliva secreted into the oral cavity contains electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻) and enzymes, salivary amylase and lysozyme; the chemical process of digestion is initiated in the oral cavity by the hydrolytic action of the carbohydrate-splitting enzyme, the salivary amylase; about 30 per cent of starch is hydrolysed here by this enzyme (optimum pH 6.8) into a disaccharide, maltose; lysozyme present in saliva acts as an antibacterial agent that prevents infections. The mucosa of the stomach has gastric glands, which have three major types of cells: mucus neck cells, which secrete mucus; peptic or chief cells, which secrete the proenzyme pepsinogen; and parietal or oxyntic cells, which secrete HCl and intrinsic factor (needed for absorption of vitamin B₁₂); pepsinogen, on exposure to hydrochloric acid, gets converted into the active enzyme pepsin, the proteolytic enzyme of the stomach; pepsin converts proteins into proteoses and peptones; HCl provides the acidic pH (pH 1.8) optimal for pepsins. The bile released into the duodenum contains bile pigments (bilirubin and biliverdin), bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids, but no enzymes; bile helps in emulsification of fats, i.e. breaking down of the fats into very small micelles; bile also activates lipases. The pancreatic juice contains inactive enzymes — trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases, amylases, lipases and nucleases; trypsinogen is activated by an enzyme, enterokinase, secreted by the intestinal mucosa into active trypsin, which in turn activates the other enzymes in the pancreatic juice. Enzymes are proteins, so heating denatures them and extremes of pH inactivate them.
Why: Only the tube with active enzyme at a suitable pH breaks down starch, so the iodine colour disappears only there.
Why not the others: (A) Saliva contains amylase, not pepsin. (C) Bile is from the liver and acts on fats. (D) Without active enzyme, starch is not digested in this time.
Key point: Salivary amylase (pH 6.8) digests starch; enzymes are denatured by heat and inactivated by extreme pH.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing amoeboid, ciliary and muscular movement and the structure, control and locations of skeletal, visceral and cardiac muscles
questions.question: Which comparison of types of movement and muscle is correct?
options: A) Ciliary movement moves macrophages and leucocytes, while amoeboid movement clears dust from the trachea
B) Visceral muscles are striated and voluntary, found in the limbs

C) Amoeboid movement, by streaming of protoplasm and pseudopodia with microfilaments, is seen in macrophages and leucocytes; ciliary movement occurs in internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium — coordinated beats of cilia in the trachea remove dust particles and foreign substances, and in the female reproductive tract help move the ova; muscular movement moves limbs, jaws and tongue; skeletal muscles are striated and voluntary and attached to bones; visceral muscles, in the inner walls of hollow organs such as the alimentary canal and reproductive tract, are smooth (non-striated) and involuntary; cardiac muscle is striated, branched and involuntary and is found only in the heart
D) Cardiac muscle is smooth and under voluntary control
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Amoeboid, ciliary and muscular movements correctly placed; skeletal (striated, voluntary), visceral (smooth, involuntary), cardiac (striated, involuntary).
Concept: Cells of the human body exhibit three main types of movements, namely amoeboid, ciliary and muscular. Some specialised cells in our body like macrophages and leucocytes in blood exhibit amoeboid movement; it is effected by pseudopodia formed by the streaming of protoplasm (as in Amoeba); cytoskeletal elements like microfilaments are also involved in amoeboid movement. Ciliary movement occurs in most of our internal tubular organs which are lined by ciliated epithelium; the coordinated movements of cilia in the trachea help us in removing dust particles and some of the foreign substances inhaled along with the atmospheric air; passage of ova through the female reproductive tract is also facilitated by ciliary movement. Movement of our limbs, jaws, tongue, etc., requires muscular movement; the contractile property of muscles is effectively used for locomotion and other movements by human beings and the majority of multicellular organisms. Muscles have been classified using different criteria, namely location, appearance and nature of regulation of their activities; based on their location, three types of muscles are identified: (i) skeletal, (ii) visceral and (iii) cardiac. Skeletal muscles are closely associated with the skeletal components of the body; they have a striped appearance under the microscope and hence are called striated muscles; as their activities are under the voluntary control of the nervous system, they are known as voluntary muscles too; they are primarily involved in locomotory actions and changes of body postures. Visceral muscles are located in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs of the body like the alimentary canal, reproductive tract, etc.; they do not exhibit any striation and are smooth in appearance; hence, they are called smooth muscles (non-striated muscles); their activities are not under the voluntary control of the nervous system and they are therefore known as involuntary muscles; they assist, for example, in the transportation of food through the digestive tract and gametes through the genital tract. As the name suggests, cardiac muscles are the muscles of the heart; many cardiac muscle cells assemble in a branching pattern to form a cardiac muscle; based on appearance, cardiac muscles are striated; they are involuntary in nature as the nervous system does not control their activities directly.
Why: Each type of movement and muscle is suited to its site — moving cells, moving fluid over surfaces, or moving body parts.
Why not the others: (A) The two movement types are swapped. (B) Visceral muscles are smooth and involuntary. (D) Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary.
Key point: Skeletal: striated, voluntary; visceral: smooth, involuntary; cardiac: striated, involuntary.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the effects of damage to different regions of the human brain from their known functions
questions.question: Three patients have localised brain injuries. Patient X walks unsteadily and cannot coordinate quick movements. Patient Y has irregular breathing and heartbeat. Patient Z has lost control of body temperature, hunger and thirst. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) X has damage to the cerebellum, which integrates information from the semicircular canals of the ear and the auditory system and coordinates movement; Y has damage to the medulla, which contains centres controlling respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions; Z has damage to the hypothalamus, which contains centres controlling body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking and also has neurosecretory cells that release hypothalamic hormones; the cerebral hemispheres, joined by the corpus callosum, handle sensory perception, voluntary motor control, memory and communication, and the limbic system with the hypothalamus regulates sexual behaviour and emotions
B) X has damage to the medulla and Y to the cerebellum
C) Z has damage to the cerebellum, which controls hunger and thirst
D) All three injuries are in the spinal cord, since the brain does not control these functions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X cerebellum, Y medulla, Z hypothalamus.
Concept: The human brain can be divided into three major parts: forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain. The forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus; the cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain; a deep cleft divides the cerebrum longitudinally into two halves, termed the left and right cerebral hemispheres, connected by a tract of nerve fibres called the corpus callosum; the cerebral cortex contains motor areas, sensory areas and large regions that are neither clearly sensory nor motor in function, called the association areas, responsible for complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication. The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus and contains a number of centres which control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking; it also contains several groups of neurosecretory cells which secrete hormones called hypothalamic hormones. The inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres and a group of associated deep structures like the amygdala and hippocampus form a complex structure called the limbic lobe or limbic system; along with the hypothalamus, it is involved in the regulation of sexual behaviour, expression of emotional reactions (e.g. excitement, pleasure, rage and fear) and motivation. The hindbrain comprises the pons, cerebellum and medulla (also called the medulla oblongata); pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain; the cerebellum has a very convoluted surface in order to provide additional space for many more neurons; the medulla of the brain is connected to the spinal cord and contains centres which control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. The cerebellum integrates information received from the semicircular canals of the ear and the auditory system, which is why its damage disturbs balance and coordination.
Why: Each brain region has a specific set of centres, so damage to it produces a specific set of symptoms.
Why not the others: (B) Cerebellum and medulla functions swapped. (C) Hunger and thirst centres are in the hypothalamus. (D) These functions are controlled by brain centres.
Key point: Cerebellum — coordination and balance; medulla — breathing and heart; hypothalamus — temperature, hunger, thirst.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating reaction enthalpy from bond enthalpies and mean C–H bond enthalpy from atomization enthalpy, and interpreting the enthalpy of solution of an ionic solid as lattice and hydration terms
questions.question: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 435, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. The enthalpy of atomization of CH₄ is 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. When NaCl dissolves in water in a calorimeter, the temperature falls slightly. Which set of results is correct?
options: A) ΔrH(H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl) = +185 kJ; mean C–H = 1665 kJ mol⁻¹; dissolution of NaCl is exothermic
B) ΔrH = −246 kJ; mean C–H = 555 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH − ΔhydH, so it is always negative

C) ΔrH = (435 + 242) − 2(431) = −185 kJ for 2 mol HCl; mean C–H bond enthalpy = 1665/4 ≈ 416 kJ mol⁻¹; the small cooling shows ΔsolH of NaCl is slightly positive, since ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH and the energy needed to break the lattice (+788 kJ mol⁻¹) is slightly more than the energy released on hydration of the ions (−784 kJ mol⁻¹)
D) ΔrH = −431 kJ; mean C–H = 416 kJ mol⁻¹; NaCl does not interact with water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ΔrH = −185 kJ; mean C–H ≈ 416 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔsolH of NaCl slightly positive.
Concept: Chemical reactions involve the breaking and making of chemical bonds; energy is required to break a bond and energy is released when a bond is formed. For gaseous reactions, ΔrH = Σ bond enthalpies of reactants − Σ bond enthalpies of products; this relationship is approximate and valid when all substances are gases. Bond dissociation enthalpy of a diatomic molecule is the enthalpy change on breaking one mole of its bonds in the gas phase; in polyatomic molecules such as methane, the four C–H bonds are not broken with the same energy, so the mean bond enthalpy is used: ΔaH(CH₄) = 1665 kJ mol⁻¹ for CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g), so ΔC–H H = ¼ × 1665 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹. Enthalpy of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance dissolves in a specified amount of solvent; for an ionic compound, dissolution may be considered to take place in two steps — breaking the lattice into gaseous ions (lattice enthalpy, positive) and hydration of the gaseous ions (hydration enthalpy, negative): ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH; for NaCl(s), ΔsolH = +788 − 784 = +4 kJ mol⁻¹, so the dissolution of NaCl is accompanied by very little heat change; for most ionic compounds ΔsolH is positive and the dissociation process is endothermic, so solubility increases with temperature.
Given: Bond enthalpies; ΔaH(CH₄) = 1665 kJ mol⁻¹; observed cooling.
Formula/Principle: ΔrH = Σ BE(broken) − Σ BE(formed); ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH.
Step 1: Bonds broken: H–H + Cl–Cl = 677 kJ; formed: 2 H–Cl = 862 kJ.
Step 2: ΔrH = 677 − 862 = −185 kJ.
Step 3: C–H = 1665/4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹; cooling ⇒ ΔsolH > 0 (788 > 784).
Why: More energy is released forming the two H–Cl bonds than is used breaking H–H and Cl–Cl, and for NaCl lattice breaking narrowly outweighs hydration.
Why not the others: (A) Sign reversed; atomization covers four bonds; cooling means endothermic. (B) Arithmetic wrong; the hydration term is added and ΔsolH can be positive. (D) Uses one bond only; ions are hydrated by water.
Key point: ΔrH = bonds broken − bonds formed; ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining why successive ionisation constants of polybasic acids decrease, and how bond strength and electronegativity decide acid strength in a group and across a period
questions.question: Which explanation of polybasic acids and acid strength is correct?
options: A) For carbonic acid Ka1 = 4.3 × 10⁻⁷ and Ka2 = 5.6 × 10⁻¹¹; Ka2 is much smaller because removing a positively charged proton from the negatively charged HCO₃⁻ ion is much harder than from neutral H₂CO₃, so for polybasic acids Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3 and [H⁺] comes mainly from the first step; among HF, HCl, HBr and HI acid strength increases down the group because the H–X bond becomes weaker as the size of X increases, while across a period (CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF) acid strength increases with the electronegativity of the atom bonded to H
