B) Ka2 is larger than Ka1 because the anion holds the second proton loosely
C) HF is the strongest of the hydrogen halides because fluorine is the most electronegative
D) Across a period acid strength decreases as electronegativity increases
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ka1 ≫ Ka2 for H₂CO₃; HI strongest halide acid (weakest bond); acidity increases with electronegativity across a period.
Concept: Some acids like oxalic acid, sulphuric acid and phosphoric acid have more than one ionisable proton per molecule; such acids are known as polybasic or polyprotic acids; for a dibasic acid H₂X, the ionisation reactions are H₂X ⇌ H⁺ + HX⁻ (Ka1) and HX⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + X²⁻ (Ka2); it can be seen that higher-order ionisation constants (Ka2, Ka3) are smaller than the lower-order ionisation constant (Ka1) of a polyprotic acid; the reason is that it is more difficult to remove a positively charged proton from a negative ion due to electrostatic forces. The extent of dissociation of an acid depends on the strength and polarity of the H–A bond; in general, when the strength of the H–A bond decreases, that is, the energy required to break the bond decreases, HA becomes a stronger acid; also, when the H–A bond becomes more polar, i.e. the electronegativity difference between H and A increases, there is marked charge separation and cleavage of the bond becomes easier, thereby increasing the acidity. When elements in the same group of the periodic table are compared, the H–A bond strength is a more important factor in determining acidity than its polar nature; as the size of A increases down the group, H–A bond strength decreases and so the acid strength increases: HF ≪ HCl < HBr < HI. When elements in the same row of the periodic table are compared, H–A bond polarity becomes the deciding factor; as the electronegativity of A increases, the strength of the acid also increases: CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF.
Why: The second proton must leave an already negative ion, and acid strength depends on how easily the H–A bond breaks to give H⁺.
Why not the others: (B) Ka2 is smaller. (C) HF has the strongest H–X bond and is the weakest acid of the group. (D) Across a period acidity increases with electronegativity.
Key point: Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3; down a group bond strength decides, across a period polarity decides.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting whether salt solutions are acidic, basic or neutral from the strength of the parent acid and base, and calculating the pH of a salt of a weak acid and strong base
questions.question: Which set of predictions about aqueous salt solutions is correct? (pKa of CH₃COOH = 4.74)
options: A) NaCl acidic; CH₃COONa neutral; NH₄Cl basic; CH₃COONH₄ strongly basic
B) All salts give neutral solutions because they are formed by neutralisation
C) NH₄Cl solution is basic because NH₄⁺ releases OH⁻; pH of 0.10 M CH₃COONa is 4.74

D) NaCl gives a neutral solution (no hydrolysis); CH₃COONa is basic (CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻); NH₄Cl is acidic (NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄OH + H⁺); for CH₃COONH₄ both ions hydrolyse and pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb) ≈ 7; and the pH of 0.10 M CH₃COONa is 7 + ½(pKa + log C) = 7 + ½(4.74 − 1) ≈ 8.87
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) NaCl neutral, CH₃COONa basic, NH₄Cl acidic, CH₃COONH₄ about neutral; pH of 0.10 M CH₃COONa ≈ 8.87.
Concept: Salts formed by the reactions between acids and bases in definite proportions undergo ionisation in water; the cations/anions formed on ionisation of salts either exist as hydrated ions in aqueous solutions or interact with water to re-form the corresponding acids/bases depending upon the nature of the salts; the latter process of interaction between water and cations/anions or both of salts is called hydrolysis; the pH of the solution gets affected by this interaction. The cations (e.g. Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺) of strong bases and anions (e.g. Cl⁻, Br⁻, NO₃⁻, ClO₄⁻) of strong acids simply get hydrated but do not hydrolyse, and therefore the solutions of salts formed from strong acids and bases are neutral, i.e. their pH is 7. Salts of weak acid and strong base, e.g. CH₃COONa, are basic in nature: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻; acetic acid, being a weak acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), remains mainly unionised, and the increase of OH⁻ concentration makes the solution alkaline. Similarly, NH₄Cl, formed from a weak base NH₄OH and a strong acid HCl, dissociates completely in water: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄OH + H⁺; ammonium hydroxide is a weak base (Kb = 1.77 × 10⁻⁵) and therefore remains almost unionised, which results in an increase of H⁺ ion concentration and makes the solution acidic. For a salt of weak acid and weak base, both ions hydrolyse and pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb); it may be more or less than 7 depending on Ka and Kb, and for ammonium acetate, where pKa ≈ pKb, it is close to 7. For a salt of a weak acid and strong base, pH = 7 + ½(pKa + log C).
Given: pKa = 4.74, C = 0.10 M.
Formula/Principle: pH = 7 + ½(pKa + log C).
Step 1: log 0.10 = −1.
Step 2: pKa + log C = 3.74.
Step 3: pH = 7 + 1.87 = 8.87.
Why: Only ions derived from weak acids or weak bases react with water, shifting the balance of H⁺ and OH⁻.
Why not the others: (A) Predictions reversed. (B) Hydrolysis makes many salt solutions non-neutral. (C) NH₄⁺ releases H⁺; CH₃COONa solution is basic.
Key point: Strong–strong neutral; weak acid–strong base basic; strong acid–weak base acidic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Balancing the oxidation of iodide by acidified dichromate by the ion-electron method and using the titration of liberated iodine with thiosulphate to relate moles
questions.question: Acidified potassium dichromate is added to excess KI; the orange solution turns green and iodine is liberated, which is then titrated with sodium thiosulphate using starch. Which balanced equation and mole relationship are correct?
options: A) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + I₂ + H₂O; 1 mol dichromate needs 2 mol thiosulphate

B) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6I⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O, the orange-to-green change showing reduction of Cr(+6) to Cr(+3) while I⁻ (−1) is oxidised to I₂ (0); then I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻, so 1 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 3 mol I₂ → 6 mol S₂O₃²⁻
C) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3I⁻ + 7H⁺ → Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O; 1 mol dichromate needs 3 mol thiosulphate
D) Dichromate is oxidised to chromate and iodine is reduced; no titration relationship exists
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6I⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O; 1 : 3 : 6 for dichromate : iodine : thiosulphate.
Concept: In the half-reaction (ion-electron) method, the two half equations are balanced separately and then added together to give the balanced equation; steps: write the oxidation and reduction half reactions; balance atoms other than O and H; balance O by adding H₂O and H by adding H⁺ (in acidic medium); balance charge by adding electrons; multiply to equalise electrons and add. Potassium dichromate is a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O; the orange colour of dichromate changes to the green colour of Cr³⁺. Iodide is oxidised: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻. The liberated iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulphate (iodometry), with starch as indicator: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻; the blue colour of the starch–iodine complex disappears at the end point.
Given: Cr₂O₇²⁻/Cr³⁺ and I⁻/I₂ in acid; I₂ titrated with S₂O₃²⁻.
Formula/Principle: Electrons lost = electrons gained; balance O with H₂O, H with H⁺.
Step 1: Reduction: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.
Step 2: Oxidation ×3: 6I⁻ → 3I₂ + 6e⁻; add to get the net equation.
Step 3: 3I₂ react with 6S₂O₃²⁻ ⇒ 1 : 6 overall.
Why: Each Cr atom gains 3 electrons, so one dichromate (two Cr) accepts 6 electrons, oxidising six iodide ions to three I₂ molecules.
Why not the others: (A) Electrons and charge are not balanced. (C) Chromium atoms are not balanced. (D) Dichromate is reduced and iodide oxidised.
Key point: Cr₂O₇²⁻ accepts 6e⁻; 1 Cr₂O₇²⁻ ≡ 3I₂ ≡ 6S₂O₃²⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the stability orders and shapes of carbocations, carbanions and free radicals and explaining them through inductive effect, hyperconjugation and resonance
questions.question: Which statement about reactive intermediates is correct?
options: A) Carbocation stability is 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ because of the +I effect and hyperconjugation of alkyl groups, and benzyl and allyl cations are further stabilised by resonance; a carbocation is sp² hybridised and planar with an empty p orbital; carbanions follow the reverse order CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3°, because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilise the negative charge, and a simple carbanion is sp³ hybridised and pyramidal; free radicals, with one unpaired electron, follow the order 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃•
B) Carbanions and carbocations follow the same stability order, 3° most stable
C) A carbocation is sp³ hybridised and pyramidal, carrying a lone pair
D) Free radicals are formed by heterolytic cleavage of a covalent bond
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Carbocations 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ (planar, sp²); carbanions reverse (pyramidal, sp³); radicals 3° > 2° > 1°.
Concept: A covalent bond can be cleaved either by heterolytic cleavage or by homolytic cleavage; in heterolytic cleavage the bond breaks in such a fashion that the shared pair of electrons remains with one of the fragments; a species having a carbon atom possessing a sextet of electrons and a positive charge is called a carbocation; carbocations are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary; the observed order of carbocation stability is CH₃⁺ < CH₃CH₂⁺ < (CH₃)₂CH⁺ < (CH₃)₃C⁺; these carbocations have trigonal planar shape with the positively charged carbon being sp² hybridised, with an unhybridised p orbital which remains vacant perpendicular to the molecular plane. Alkyl groups stabilise carbocations by the inductive effect and hyperconjugation: hyperconjugation is a general stabilising interaction involving delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond of an alkyl group directly attached to an atom of an unsaturated system or to an atom with an unshared p orbital; the greater the number of alkyl groups attached to a positively charged carbon atom, the greater the hyperconjugation interaction and stabilisation of the cation. Heterolytic cleavage can also give a species in which carbon gets the shared pair of electrons, called a carbanion; carbanions are also unstable and reactive species; the carbon in a carbanion is sp³ hybridised and its structure is distorted tetrahedral (pyramidal), with the lone pair occupying one position; electron-donating alkyl groups destabilise the carbanion, so the order is the reverse of carbocations. In homolytic cleavage, one of the electrons of the shared pair goes with each of the bonded atoms, giving neutral species with an unpaired electron, called free radicals; like carbocations, alkyl radicals are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary, and alkyl radical stability increases as we proceed from primary to tertiary. Allyl and benzyl cations, radicals and anions are stabilised by resonance.
Why: Alkyl groups push electron density towards carbon, which helps an electron-deficient centre but hurts an electron-rich one.
Why not the others: (B) Carbanion order is the reverse. (C) Carbocations are planar sp² with an empty p orbital. (D) Free radicals come from homolytic cleavage.
Key point: Electron donors stabilise C⁺ and C•, destabilise C⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of substituents on benzene to decide which entries for directing influence and activation are correct
questions.question:
A student lists substituents with their effect on further electrophilic substitution:

Substituent | Directs to | Effect on ring
1. –OH | ortho, para | activating
2. –CH₃ | ortho, para | activating
3. –NO₂ | ortho, para | deactivating
4. –Cl | meta | activating
5. –CHO | meta | deactivating
6. –NH₂ | ortho, para | activating

How many rows are fully correct?
options: A) All 6
B) 3 (rows 1, 2 and 6)
C) 5 (all except row 4)

D) 4 (rows 1, 2, 5 and 6); –NO₂ is meta-directing and deactivating because it withdraws electrons by –R and –I effects, making the ortho and para positions most electron-poor; –Cl is ortho, para-directing (lone pairs donate by +R) but deactivating, because its strong –I effect outweighs the +R effect
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Four rows correct; rows 3 and 4 are wrong.
Concept: When monosubstituted benzene is subjected to further substitution, three possible disubstituted products are not formed in equal amounts; two types of behaviour are observed — either ortho and para products or the meta product is predominantly formed; this behaviour depends on the nature of the substituent already present in the benzene ring and not on the nature of the entering group; this is known as the directive influence of substituents. Ortho and para directing groups: the groups which direct the incoming group to ortho and para positions are called ortho and para directing groups, e.g. –OH, –NH₂, –NHR, –NHCOCH₃, –OCH₃, –CH₃, –C₂H₅; in phenol, the –OH group donates electrons by +R effect, increasing electron density at ortho and para positions more than at the meta position, and these groups activate the ring for electrophilic substitution; –CH₃ activates by +I effect and hyperconjugation. Meta directing groups: groups that direct the incoming group to the meta position, e.g. –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO₃H; in nitrobenzene, the nitro group reduces the electron density in the benzene ring due to its strong –I and –R effects, and the electron density is reduced more at ortho and para positions, so the meta position is relatively electron-rich and electrophilic attack occurs there; such groups also deactivate the ring. Halogens are deactivating because of their strong –I effect, and the overall electron density on the benzene ring decreases, making further substitution difficult; however, due to resonance (+R) the electron density on ortho and para positions is greater than at the meta position, so they are also ortho and para directing.
Given: Six rows.
Formula/Principle: +R/+I donors (except halogens) activate and direct o/p; –R/–I acceptors deactivate and direct m; halogens deactivate but direct o/p.
Step 1: Rows 1, 2, 6 correct (donors).
Step 2: Row 5 correct (–CHO meta, deactivating).
Step 3: Row 3 wrong (–NO₂ is meta); row 4 wrong (–Cl is o/p, deactivating) ⇒ 4 correct.
Why: Directing effect follows where electron density is highest in the ring, while activation follows the overall electron density.
Why not the others: (A) Rows 3 and 4 are wrong. (B) Row 5 is also correct. (C) Row 3 is also wrong.
Key point: Halogens: o/p directing but deactivating; –NO₂, –CHO, –COOH: meta, deactivating.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the energies of ethane conformations, and using the product ratio from free-radical chlorination of propane to find the relative reactivity of secondary and primary hydrogens
questions.question: The staggered and eclipsed conformations of ethane differ in energy by about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Photochemical chlorination of propane gives 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane in the ratio 45 : 55. What is the reactivity of a secondary hydrogen relative to a primary hydrogen, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 1.2; the eclipsed form is more stable, and chlorination is an ionic reaction

B) About 3.7 (per H: 55/2 = 27.5 for the two 2° H against 45/6 = 7.5 for the six 1° H); the staggered form is more stable because torsional strain from repulsion between bond pairs is least, but the small energy difference means the forms interconvert freely and cannot be isolated at room temperature; chlorination proceeds by a free-radical chain — initiation (homolysis of Cl₂ by light), propagation (Cl• abstracts H to give an alkyl radical that reacts with Cl₂) and termination (radicals combine)
C) 0.82; the conformations can be separated at room temperature
D) 11; propagation consists of two radicals combining
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Relative reactivity ≈ 3.7; staggered more stable but freely interconverting; free-radical chain mechanism.
Concept: Alkanes contain carbon–carbon sigma bonds; electron distribution of the sigma molecular orbital is symmetrical around the internuclear axis of the C–C bond, which is not disturbed by rotation about its axis; this permits free rotation about a C–C single bond, giving rise to different spatial arrangements of atoms called conformations; ethane has an infinite number of conformations, of which the staggered (hydrogens of the two carbons as far apart as possible) and eclipsed (hydrogens of the two carbons as close as possible) are the extremes, represented in Sawhorse and Newman projections; in the staggered form the electron clouds of carbon–hydrogen bonds are as far apart as possible, so there are minimum repulsive forces, minimum energy and maximum stability; the repulsive interaction between electron clouds, which affects the stability of a conformation, is called torsional strain; the energy difference between the two extreme forms is of the order of 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, which is very small, so even at ordinary temperatures the molecules gain enough thermal or kinetic energy to overcome this barrier through intermolecular collisions; thus it is not possible to separate and isolate different conformational isomers of ethane. Halogenation of alkanes takes place in the presence of diffused sunlight or ultraviolet light or at high temperature; the reaction proceeds via a free-radical chain mechanism: (i) initiation — homolysis of the Cl–Cl bond in the presence of light or heat gives chlorine free radicals; (ii) propagation — a chlorine free radical attacks the alkane molecule, breaking the C–H bond to generate a methyl or alkyl free radical with formation of H–Cl, and the alkyl radical attacks a second chlorine molecule to form alkyl chloride with liberation of a chlorine free radical; (iii) termination — the reaction stops after some time due to consumption of reactants or combination of radicals. Propane has six primary and two secondary hydrogens; the product ratio divided by the number of each type of hydrogen gives the reactivity per hydrogen.
Given: Product ratio 45 : 55; 6 primary H, 2 secondary H.
Formula/Principle: Relative reactivity per H = (fraction of product)/(number of such H).
Step 1: Per primary H: 45/6 = 7.5.
Step 2: Per secondary H: 55/2 = 27.5.
Step 3: Ratio = 27.5/7.5 ≈ 3.7.
Why: Secondary radicals are more stable than primary ones, so secondary hydrogens are abstracted faster even though there are fewer of them.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the number of hydrogens; staggered is more stable; the mechanism is free radical. (C) Ratio inverted; conformations cannot be isolated. (D) Combination of radicals is termination.
Key point: Reactivity per H = product share/number of H; staggered ethane more stable by about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using the Nernst equation to find the emf of a Daniell cell with unequal concentrations and the potential of a hydrogen electrode at a given pH
questions.question: For Zn | Zn²⁺(0.001 M) || Cu²⁺(0.10 M) | Cu with E°cell = 1.10 V at 298 K, what is Ecell? What is the potential of a hydrogen electrode (1 bar H₂) dipped in a solution of pH 10, and how does Ecell of the Daniell cell change if [Cu²⁺] is raised?
options: A) 1.04 V; +0.59 V; Ecell decreases
B) 1.10 V; 0 V; Ecell is unchanged since E° is fixed
C) Ecell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log(0.001/0.10) = 1.10 + 0.059 = 1.159 V; E(H⁺/H₂) = −0.059 × pH = −0.59 V; raising [Cu²⁺] increases Ecell, because the reaction quotient Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] falls
D) 1.21 V; −0.059 V; Ecell decreases
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ecell ≈ 1.16 V; E = −0.59 V; Ecell rises with [Cu²⁺].
Concept: Nernst showed that for the electrode reaction Mⁿ⁺(aq) + ne⁻ → M(s), the electrode potential at any concentration measured with respect to the standard hydrogen electrode is E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(1/[Mⁿ⁺]). For a cell, Ecell = E°cell − (2.303RT/nF) log Q, which at 298 K becomes Ecell = E°cell − (0.059/n) log Q. For the Daniell cell, Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), n = 2 and Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]; it can be seen that Ecell increases with increase in the concentration of Cu²⁺ ions and decrease in the concentration of Zn²⁺ ions. For the hydrogen electrode, H⁺ + e⁻ → ½H₂, E = 0 − 0.059 log(1/[H⁺]) = −0.059 pH (at 1 bar H₂).
Given: [Zn²⁺] = 0.001 M, [Cu²⁺] = 0.10 M, E° = 1.10 V, n = 2; pH 10.
Formula/Principle: Ecell = E° − (0.059/n) log Q.
Step 1: Q = 0.001/0.10 = 10⁻²; log Q = −2.
Step 2: Ecell = 1.10 − (0.059/2)(−2) = 1.10 + 0.059 = 1.159 V.
Step 3: E(H) = −0.059 × 10 = −0.59 V.
Why: A product concentration below the reactant concentration pushes the reaction forward, raising the cell voltage above E°.
Why not the others: (A) Sign of the log term wrong; E(H) is negative at pH 10. (B) Ecell depends on concentrations. (D) Wrong magnitudes and direction.
Key point: Ecell = E° − (0.059/n) log Q; E(H⁺/H₂) = −0.059 pH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the collision theory rate expression with orientation factor, and calculating how much a catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering activation energy while leaving equilibrium unchanged
questions.question: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction by 10 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; e⁴ ≈ 55). By roughly what factor does the rate increase, and which statement about collision theory and catalysts is correct?
options: A) About 2 times; a catalyst shifts the equilibrium towards products
B) About 4 times; every collision between reactant molecules leads to reaction
C) About 1000 times; a catalyst changes ΔG of the reaction

D) About 55 times (k ∝ e^{−Ea/RT}, so the ratio is e^{10000/(8.314 × 300)} = e^{4.0}); by collision theory rate = P Z_AB e^{−Ea/RT}, where Z_AB is the collision frequency, the Boltzmann factor gives the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea and P is the probability or steric factor for proper orientation; a catalyst provides an alternative path of lower activation energy, speeds forward and backward reactions equally, and does not change ΔG or the equilibrium constant, only helping equilibrium to be reached sooner
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) About 55 times; rate = P Z_AB e^{−Ea/RT}; catalysts lower Ea without changing ΔG or K.
Concept: Collision theory, developed by Max Trautz and William Lewis, is based on the kinetic theory of gases; reactant molecules are assumed to be hard spheres, and reaction is postulated to occur when molecules collide with each other; the number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture is the collision frequency (Z); another factor which affects the rate is activation energy; for a bimolecular elementary reaction, rate = Z_AB e^{−Ea/RT}; however, not all molecules with sufficient energy react; proper orientation of reactant molecules leads to bond formation whereas improper orientation makes them simply bounce back; to account for effective collisions, another factor P, called the probability or steric factor, is introduced: rate = P Z_AB e^{−Ea/RT}. A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change; according to intermediate complex theory, a catalyst participates in a chemical reaction by forming temporary bonds with the reactants, resulting in an intermediate complex with a transitory existence that decomposes to yield products and the catalyst; a catalyst provides an alternate pathway or reaction mechanism by reducing the activation energy between reactants and products; a catalyst does not alter Gibbs energy, ΔG, of a reaction; it catalyses spontaneous reactions but does not catalyse non-spontaneous reactions; a catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reaction; rather, it helps in attaining the equilibrium faster, that is, it catalyses the forward as well as the backward reactions to the same extent, so that the equilibrium state remains the same but is reached earlier.
Given: ΔEa = −10 kJ mol⁻¹, T = 300 K.
Formula/Principle: k₂/k₁ = e^{(Ea1 − Ea2)/RT}.
Step 1: (Ea1 − Ea2)/RT = 10 000/(8.314 × 300) = 10 000/2494 = 4.01.
Step 2: k₂/k₁ = e^{4.01} ≈ 55.
Step 3: Equilibrium constant unchanged since forward and backward rates rise equally.
Why: Lowering the barrier increases exponentially the fraction of molecules with enough energy, for both directions alike.
Why not the others: (A) Factor too small; equilibrium is not shifted. (B) Only collisions with enough energy and proper orientation react. (C) Factor too large; ΔG is unchanged.
Key point: Rate = P Z e^{−Ea/RT}; catalyst lowers Ea, leaves ΔG and K unchanged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing actinides with lanthanides in oxidation states, contraction, radioactivity and chemical reactivity, with reasons based on 4f and 5f orbitals
questions.question: Which comparison of actinides with lanthanides is correct?
options: A) Actinides show a much wider range of oxidation states (up to +7, e.g. in Np and Pu) than lanthanides (mainly +3, with Ce⁴⁺ an oxidant and Eu²⁺, Yb²⁺ reductants), because the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies; the actinide contraction is greater from element to element than the lanthanide contraction, owing to poorer shielding by 5f electrons; all actinides are radioactive, many with short half-lives, which makes their study difficult; and actinide metals are highly reactive, especially when finely divided
B) Lanthanides show more oxidation states than actinides because 4f electrons are less tightly held
C) The lanthanide contraction is greater than the actinide contraction because 4f electrons shield very poorly compared with 5f
D) Actinides are non-radioactive and chemically inert
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Actinides: wider oxidation-state range, greater contraction, radioactive, reactive.
Concept: The lanthanoids are the 14 elements following lanthanum, and the actinoids the 14 elements following actinium, in which the 4f and 5f orbitals respectively are progressively filled. In the lanthanoids, La(III) and Ln(III) compounds are predominant; however, occasionally +2 and +4 ions in solution or in solid compounds are also obtained; this irregularity arises mainly from the extra stability of empty, half-filled or filled f subshells; Ce(IV) is favoured by its noble gas configuration but is a strong oxidant reverting to the common +3 state; Eu²⁺ and Yb²⁺ are strong reducing agents changing to the common +3 state. The actinoids show in general +3 oxidation state, but the elements in the first half of the series frequently exhibit higher oxidation states; for example, the maximum oxidation state increases from +4 in Th to +5, +6 and +7 respectively in Pa, U and Np, but decreases in succeeding elements; the actinoids resemble the lanthanoids in having more compounds in the +3 state than in the +4 state; this wider range is attributed to the fact that the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies. There is a gradual decrease in the size of atoms or M³⁺ ions across the actinoid series, which may be referred to as the actinoid contraction (like lanthanoid contraction); the contraction is, however, greater from element to element in this series, resulting from poor shielding by 5f electrons. The actinoids are radioactive elements, and the earlier members have relatively long half-lives while the latter ones have half-life values ranging from a day to 3 minutes for lawrencium (Z = 103); the latter members could be prepared only in nanogram quantities, so their study is difficult. The actinoid metals are all silvery in appearance but display a variety of structures; they are highly reactive metals, especially when finely divided; the action of boiling water on them, for example, gives a mixture of oxide and hydride, and combination with most non-metals takes place at moderate temperatures.
Why: The 5f orbitals extend further and lie close in energy to 6d and 7s, so more electrons can take part in bonding, while shielding by 5f electrons is poorer.
Why not the others: (B) Actinides show more oxidation states. (C) The actinide contraction is greater. (D) All actinides are radioactive and reactive.
Key point: Actinides: more oxidation states (5f ≈ 6d ≈ 7s), larger contraction, radioactive.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting moles of AgCl precipitated from cobalt(III) ammine chlorides with excess silver nitrate in terms of Werner's primary and secondary valences
questions.question: One mole each of three complexes is treated with excess AgNO₃ at room temperature: CoCl₃·6NH₃ gives 3 mol AgCl, CoCl₃·5NH₃ gives 2 mol and CoCl₃·4NH₃ gives 1 mol. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) All chlorides are bound to cobalt in each complex, so AgCl forms from decomposition

B) The formulae are [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ and [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl; by Werner's theory, the primary valence (here +3, the oxidation state) is satisfied by ionisable chloride ions that precipitate as AgCl, while the secondary valence (coordination number 6) is satisfied by the ligands NH₃ and Cl⁻ bound in the coordination sphere, which do not ionise; the molar conductivities decrease in the order 1 : 3 > 1 : 2 > 1 : 1 electrolytes, and the secondary valences are directed in space, giving an octahedral shape
C) The secondary valence is ionisable and the primary valence is non-ionisable
D) The coordination number of cobalt is 3 in every complex
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂, [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl; ionisable chloride = primary valence; coordination number 6.
Concept: Alfred Werner (1898) prepared and characterised a large number of coordination compounds and studied their physical and chemical behaviour by simple experimental techniques; he observed that the number of chloride ions precipitated as AgCl, on adding excess silver nitrate solution in the cold, differed for different cobalt(III) chloride–ammonia complexes: CoCl₃·6NH₃ gives 3 mol AgCl, CoCl₃·5NH₃ gives 2 mol and CoCl₃·4NH₃ gives 1 mol; these observations, together with the results of conductivity measurements in solution, can be explained if (i) six groups in all, either chloride ions or ammonia molecules or both, remain bonded to the cobalt ion during the reaction and (ii) the compounds are formulated as [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺3Cl⁻, [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺2Cl⁻ and [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺Cl⁻, where the atoms within the square brackets form a single entity which does not dissociate under the reaction conditions. Werner proposed the concept of a primary valence and a secondary valence for a metal ion: (1) in coordination compounds metals show two types of linkages (valences) — primary and secondary; (2) the primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions; (3) the secondary valences are non-ionisable; these are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions; the secondary valence is equal to the coordination number and is fixed for a metal; (4) the ions or groups bound by the secondary linkages to the metal have characteristic spatial arrangements corresponding to different coordination numbers; in modern formulations, such spatial arrangements are called coordination polyhedra; the most common geometrical shapes are octahedral, square planar and tetrahedral.
Given: AgCl precipitated: 3, 2, 1 mol.
Formula/Principle: Moles of AgCl = number of ionisable Cl⁻ outside the coordination sphere; coordination number = 6.
Step 1: 6NH₃ fill all six positions ⇒ 3 Cl⁻ outside.
Step 2: 5NH₃ + 1 Cl inside ⇒ 2 Cl⁻ outside.
Step 3: 4NH₃ + 2 Cl inside ⇒ 1 Cl⁻ outside.
Why: Only chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are free in solution to react with Ag⁺.
Why not the others: (A) Precipitation shows some chloride is ionisable. (C) Valences reversed. (D) Coordination number is 6.
Key point: Ionisable ions = primary valence; ligands = secondary valence (coordination number).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Checking IUPAC names of coordination compounds for ligand order, ligand names, prefixes, oxidation state and anionic complex endings
questions.question:
A student writes these names:

1. K₃[Fe(CN)₆] — potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)
2. [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ — pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
3. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl(NO₂)] — diamminechloridonitrito-N-platinum(II)
4. K₂[Zn(OH)₄] — potassium tetrahydroxidozinc(II)
5. [Ni(CO)₄] — tetracarbonylnickel(II)

How many names are correct?
options: A) All 5
B) 2 (names 1 and 2)

C) 3 (names 1, 2 and 3); name 4 should be potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II), since an anionic complex takes the ending '-ate', and name 5 should be tetracarbonylnickel(0), since CO is neutral and nickel is in the zero oxidation state
D) 4 (all except name 5)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Three names correct; 4 and 5 are wrong.
Concept: Rules for naming mononuclear coordination compounds (IUPAC): (i) the cation is named first in both positively and negatively charged coordination entities; (ii) the ligands are named in alphabetical order before the name of the central atom/ion; (iii) names of anionic ligands end in -o, those of neutral and cationic ligands are the same except aqua for H₂O, ammine for NH₃, carbonyl for CO and nitrosyl for NO; anionic ligands such as Cl⁻ (chlorido), CN⁻ (cyanido), OH⁻ (hydroxido) are named accordingly; (iv) prefixes mono, di, tri, etc., are used to indicate the number of the individual ligands in the coordination entity; (v) the oxidation state of the metal in cation, anion or neutral coordination entity is indicated by a Roman numeral in parentheses; (vi) if the complex ion is a cation, the metal is named the same as the element; if the complex ion is an anion, the name of the metal ends with the suffix -ate (e.g. cobaltate, zincate; for some metals the Latin name is used, such as ferrate for Fe); (vii) the neutral complex molecule is named similar to that of the complex cation. NO₂⁻ bonded through nitrogen is named nitrito-N.
Given: Five names.
Formula/Principle: Alphabetical ligand order; -ate for anionic complexes; oxidation state from total charge.
Step 1: Name 1: [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, Fe +3, anionic ⇒ ferrate(III) ✓. Name 2: ammine before chlorido, Co +3 ✓.
Step 2: Name 3: ammine, chlorido, nitrito-N in alphabetical order, Pt +2 ✓.
Step 3: Name 4 lacks '-ate' ✗; name 5: CO neutral ⇒ Ni(0) ✗ ⇒ 3 correct.
Why: The ending and the oxidation state follow directly from the charge of the coordination entity.
Why not the others: (A) Names 4 and 5 are wrong. (B) Name 3 is also correct. (D) Name 4 is also wrong.
Key point: Anionic complex ⇒ '-ate'; neutral CO ⇒ metal oxidation state 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering alkyl halides by reactivity towards SN1 and SN2 reactions and explaining the order through steric hindrance, carbocation stability and stereochemical outcome
questions.question: Which ordering and explanation is correct?
options: A) Towards SN2, reactivity is CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°, because the nucleophile attacks from the back side and bulky groups hinder its approach to the carbon; the reaction is one-step, bimolecular and occurs with inversion of configuration; towards SN1, reactivity is 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X, because the rate-determining step is ionisation to a carbocation whose stability is greatest for 3°; benzylic and allylic halides are very reactive in SN1 because their carbocations are resonance-stabilised; SN1 is favoured by polar protic solvents and an optically active substrate gives a largely racemic product
B) SN2 reactivity is 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X, since tertiary carbocations are most stable
C) SN1 reactions occur with complete inversion of configuration in one step
D) SN1 rate depends on the concentrations of both the alkyl halide and the nucleophile
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) SN2: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric hindrance, inversion); SN1: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X (carbocation stability, racemisation).
Concept: Substitution nucleophilic bimolecular (SN2): the reaction between CH₃Cl and hydroxide ion follows second-order kinetics, i.e. the rate depends upon the concentration of both reactants; it is depicted as a single step in which the incoming nucleophile interacts with the alkyl halide, causing the carbon–halide bond to break while forming a new carbon–OH bond; these two processes take place simultaneously; as this reaction requires the approach of the nucleophile to the carbon bearing the leaving group, the presence of bulky substituents on or near the carbon atom has a dramatic inhibiting effect; of the simple alkyl halides, methyl halides react most rapidly in SN2 reactions because there are only three small hydrogen atoms; tertiary halides are the least reactive because bulky groups hinder the approaching nucleophiles; thus the order of reactivity is primary halide > secondary halide > tertiary halide; the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group, and the configuration of the carbon atom under attack inverts (Walden inversion). Substitution nucleophilic unimolecular (SN1) reactions are generally carried out in polar protic solvents (like water, alcohol, acetic acid); the reaction between tert-butyl bromide and hydroxide ion follows first-order kinetics, i.e. the rate depends upon the concentration of only one reactant, tert-butyl bromide; it occurs in two steps: in step I the polarised C–Br bond undergoes slow cleavage to produce a carbocation and a bromide ion, and the carbocation thus formed is then attacked by the nucleophile in step II to complete the substitution; step I is the slowest and reversible and is the rate-determining step; the greater the stability of the carbocation, the faster the reaction, so 3° alkyl halides undergo SN1 reaction very fast; for the same reasons, allylic and benzylic halides show high reactivity towards the SN1 reaction, as the carbocation is stabilised through resonance. In the case of optically active alkyl halides, the product formed by SN1 is a racemic mixture, because the planar carbocation can be attacked from both sides.
Why: SN2 depends on access to the carbon, while SN1 depends on how stable the carbocation intermediate is, so the two orders are opposite.
Why not the others: (B) That is the SN1 order. (C) SN1 is two-step and gives racemisation. (D) SN1 rate depends only on the alkyl halide.
Key point: SN2 — less hindered faster, inversion; SN1 — more stable carbocation faster, racemisation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols by dehydrogenation over heated copper and by oxidation with acidified dichromate
questions.question: Three isomeric alcohols C₄H₁₀O — butan-1-ol (X), butan-2-ol (Y) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (Z) — are passed over heated copper at 573 K, and separately warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Which observation and explanation is correct?
options: A) All three give aldehydes over copper and all turn dichromate green
B) X gives a ketone, Y an aldehyde and Z a carboxylic acid
C) Z is oxidised most easily because it has the most alkyl groups

D) Over copper, X (1°) is dehydrogenated to butanal and Y (2°) to butanone, while Z (3°), having no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, undergoes dehydration to 2-methylpropene; with acidified dichromate, X is oxidised to an aldehyde and then to butanoic acid, Y to butanone, and both turn the orange solution green, whereas Z resists oxidation under these conditions and the colour stays orange
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Over Cu: aldehyde, ketone, alkene; with dichromate: X and Y oxidised (green), Z not (orange).
Concept: Oxidation of alcohols involves the formation of a carbon–oxygen double bond with cleavage of an O–H and C–H bond; such a cleavage and formation of bonds occur in oxidation reactions, which are also known as dehydrogenation reactions as they involve loss of dihydrogen from an alcohol molecule. Depending on the oxidising agent used, a primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde which in turn is oxidised to a carboxylic acid; strong oxidising agents such as acidified potassium permanganate are used for getting carboxylic acids from alcohols directly; CrO₃ in anhydrous medium or pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage. Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones by chromic anhydride (CrO₃). Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation reactions; under strong reaction conditions such as strong oxidising agents (KMnO₄) and elevated temperatures, cleavage of various C–C bonds takes place and a mixture of carboxylic acids containing fewer carbon atoms is formed. When the vapours of a primary or a secondary alcohol are passed over heated copper at 573 K, dehydrogenation takes place and an aldehyde or a ketone is formed, while tertiary alcohols undergo dehydration to give alkenes. Dichromate (orange, Cr in +6) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green) when it oxidises an alcohol.
Why: Oxidation requires a hydrogen on the carbon bearing –OH; tertiary alcohols have none, so they cannot form C=O without breaking C–C bonds.
Why not the others: (A) Only X gives an aldehyde; Z is not oxidised. (B) Products of X and Y swapped; Z does not give an acid. (C) Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation.
Key point: 1° → aldehyde (→ acid), 2° → ketone, 3° → alkene over Cu, not oxidised by dichromate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Counting the products of a crossed aldol condensation, predicting the aldol and dehydration product of ethanal, and identifying aldehydes that cannot undergo aldol condensation
questions.question: A mixture of ethanal and propanal is treated with dilute NaOH. How many different β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols) can form, what are the aldol and the dehydration product from ethanal alone, and which aldehydes cannot undergo aldol condensation?
options: A) 2; 2-hydroxybutanal and butanal; ethanal and propanal

B) 4 (two self-aldols and two crossed aldols); ethanal gives 3-hydroxybutanal, which on heating loses water to give but-2-enal; methanal and benzaldehyde, which have no α-hydrogen, cannot undergo aldol condensation and instead undergo the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated alkali
C) 3; ethanal gives butanoic acid; only ketones fail to undergo aldol condensation
D) 6; ethanal gives but-1-ene; methanal undergoes aldol condensation readily
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Four aldols; 3-hydroxybutanal → but-2-enal; HCHO and C₆H₅CHO lack α-H.
Concept: The acidity of α-hydrogen atoms of carbonyl compounds is due to the strong electron-withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group and resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base. Aldehydes and ketones having at least one α-hydrogen undergo a reaction in the presence of dilute alkali as catalyst to form β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldol) or β-hydroxy ketones (ketol), respectively; this is known as the aldol reaction; the name aldol is derived from the names of the two functional groups, aldehyde and alcohol, present in the products; the aldol and ketol readily lose water to give α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compounds, which are aldol condensation products, and the reaction is called aldol condensation: 2CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO (3-hydroxybutanal) → CH₃CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal) + H₂O. When aldol condensation is carried out between two different aldehydes and/or ketones, it is called cross aldol condensation; if both of them contain α-hydrogen atoms, it gives a mixture of four products: from ethanal and propanal, 3-hydroxybutanal (ethanal + ethanal), 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal (propanal + propanal), 3-hydroxypentanal (ethanal enolate on propanal) and 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutanal (propanal enolate on ethanal). Aldehydes which do not have an α-hydrogen atom, such as formaldehyde and benzaldehyde, undergo self oxidation and reduction (disproportionation) on heating with concentrated alkali (Cannizzaro reaction).
Given: Ethanal (2 α-H positions on CH₃) and propanal (CH₂ α-carbon).
Formula/Principle: Each aldehyde with α-H can act as enolate donor and as acceptor ⇒ 2 × 2 = 4 combinations.
Step 1: Donor ethanal: on ethanal → 3-hydroxybutanal; on propanal → 3-hydroxypentanal.
Step 2: Donor propanal: on propanal → 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal; on ethanal → 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutanal.
Step 3: Total = 4.
Why: Every aldehyde with an α-hydrogen can both form an enolate and accept one, so two such aldehydes give four combinations.
Why not the others: (A) Undercounts and names wrong products. (C) Aldol gives a hydroxy aldehyde, not an acid; many ketones also react. (D) Overcounts; methanal has no α-H.
Key point: Two aldehydes with α-H ⇒ 4 aldols; no α-H ⇒ Cannizzaro.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Choosing a method of amine preparation to obtain a pure primary amine with the same, one more or one fewer carbon than the starting material
questions.question: Which statement about preparation of amines is correct?
options: A) Ammonolysis of alkyl halides gives only the primary amine, free of secondary and tertiary amines
B) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used to prepare aniline from chlorobenzene

C) Gabriel synthesis gives pure primary aliphatic amines (aryl halides fail because they do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion); reduction of nitriles (RCN with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni) gives amines with one carbon more than the alkyl halide used to make the nitrile; Hoffmann bromamide degradation of an amide (RCONH₂ with Br₂ and NaOH) gives a primary amine with one carbon fewer, so propanamide gives ethanamine; reduction of nitro compounds (e.g. with Fe and HCl) gives arylamines; and ammonolysis of alkyl halides gives a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and the quaternary salt
D) Hoffmann bromamide degradation increases the chain length by one carbon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Gabriel (pure 1° aliphatic), nitrile reduction (+1 C), Hoffmann bromamide (−1 C), nitro reduction, ammonolysis (mixture).
Concept: Nitro compounds are reduced to amines by passing hydrogen gas in the presence of finely divided nickel, palladium or platinum, and also by reduction with metals in acidic medium; reduction with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid is preferred because FeCl₂ formed gets hydrolysed to release HCl during the reaction. An alkyl or benzyl halide on reaction with an ethanolic solution of ammonia undergoes nucleophilic substitution (ammonolysis); the primary amine thus obtained behaves as a nucleophile and can further react with alkyl halide to form secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt; the disadvantage of ammonolysis is that it yields a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and also a quaternary ammonium salt. Nitriles on reduction with lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) or catalytic hydrogenation produce primary amines; this reaction is used for ascent of amine series, i.e. for preparation of amines containing one carbon atom more than the starting amine. Gabriel synthesis is used for the preparation of primary amines: phthalimide on treatment with ethanolic potassium hydroxide forms the potassium salt of phthalimide, which on heating with alkyl halide followed by alkaline hydrolysis produces the corresponding primary amine; aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by this method because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the anion formed by phthalimide. Hoffmann developed a method for preparation of primary amines by treating an amide with bromine in an aqueous or ethanolic solution of sodium hydroxide; in this degradation reaction, migration of an alkyl or aryl group takes place from the carbonyl carbon of the amide to the nitrogen atom; the amine so formed contains one carbon less than that present in the amide.
Why: Each method places the nitrogen differently, so it changes or keeps the carbon count and decides whether over-alkylation can happen.
Why not the others: (A) Ammonolysis gives a mixture. (B) Aryl halides do not react in Gabriel synthesis. (D) Hoffmann degradation removes one carbon.
Key point: Gabriel → pure 1° aliphatic amine; RCN reduction +1 C; Hoffmann bromamide −1 C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the masses of monosaccharides from hydrolysis of sucrose and explaining invert sugar, and comparing the linkages in maltose, lactose, amylose and amylopectin
questions.question: 3.42 g of sucrose (M = 342 g mol⁻¹) is completely hydrolysed. What masses of glucose and fructose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) form, why is the product called invert sugar, and which statement about other carbohydrates is correct?
options: A) 1.71 g each; the product is dextrorotatory; starch is a polymer of β-glucose
B) 3.42 g of glucose only; sucrose is a reducing sugar
C) 1.80 g of glucose only; amylose is highly branched with C1–C6 links

D) 1.80 g glucose and 1.80 g fructose (total 3.60 g, since one water molecule is added); sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the hydrolysis mixture is laevorotatory because fructose (−92.4°) rotates more strongly than glucose (+52.5°), so the sign of rotation is inverted; sucrose is non-reducing because the glycosidic bond joins C1 of α-glucose and C2 of β-fructose; maltose has two α-D-glucose units linked C1–C4 and is reducing; lactose has β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose linked C1–C4; amylose (15–20 % of starch) is an unbranched chain of α-D-glucose with C1–C4 links, while amylopectin (80–85 %) is branched through C1–C6 links
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.80 g each; invert sugar because the rotation changes sign; linkages of maltose, lactose, amylose, amylopectin.
Concept: Carbohydrates that yield two monosaccharide units on hydrolysis are called disaccharides; the two monosaccharides are joined together by an oxide linkage formed by the loss of a water molecule, called a glycosidic linkage. Sucrose is one of the common disaccharides which on hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(−)-fructose: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆; these two monosaccharides are held together by a glycosidic linkage between C1 of α-D-glucose and C2 of β-D-fructose; since the reducing groups of glucose and fructose are involved in glycosidic bond formation, sucrose is a non-reducing sugar; sucrose is dextrorotatory, but after hydrolysis gives dextrorotatory glucose and laevorotatory fructose; since the laevorotation of fructose (−92.4°) is more than the dextrorotation of glucose (+52.5°), the mixture is laevorotatory; thus hydrolysis of sucrose brings about a change in the sign of rotation, from dextro (+) to laevo (−), and the product is named invert sugar. Maltose is composed of two α-D-glucose units in which C1 of one glucose is linked to C4 of another glucose unit; the free aldehyde group can be produced at C1 of the second glucose in solution, and it shows reducing properties, so it is a reducing sugar. Lactose (milk sugar) is composed of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose; the linkage is between C1 of galactose and C4 of glucose; it is also a reducing sugar. Starch is the main storage polysaccharide of plants and a polymer of α-glucose consisting of two components — amylose and amylopectin; amylose is a water-soluble component which constitutes about 15–20 % of starch; chemically amylose is a long unbranched chain with 200–1000 α-D-(+)-glucose units held by C1–C4 glycosidic linkages; amylopectin is insoluble in water and constitutes about 80–85 % of starch; it is a branched-chain polymer of α-D-glucose units in which the chain is formed by C1–C4 glycosidic linkage whereas branching occurs by C1–C6 glycosidic linkage.
Given: 3.42 g sucrose, M = 342; M(hexose) = 180.
Formula/Principle: 1 mol sucrose + 1 mol H₂O → 1 mol glucose + 1 mol fructose.
Step 1: n(sucrose) = 3.42/342 = 0.010 mol.
Step 2: Glucose = fructose = 0.010 × 180 = 1.80 g each.
Step 3: Total 3.60 g = 3.42 g + 0.18 g of water added.
Why: Hydrolysis adds water across the glycosidic bond, so the products weigh more than the sucrose, and the stronger laevorotation of fructose flips the sign.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the added water; mixture is laevorotatory; starch is α-glucose. (B) Fructose also forms; sucrose is non-reducing. (C) Fructose also forms; amylose is unbranched.
Key point: Sucrose → glucose + fructose (invert sugar); amylose C1–C4 unbranched, amylopectin C1–C6 branches.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the limiting reagent and calculating the mass of product and of excess reagent left when hydrogen burns in oxygen
questions.question: 3.0 g of H₂ is burnt with 29.0 g of O₂ to form water (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Which result is correct?
options: A) H₂ is the limiting reagent (1.50 mol H₂ needs only 0.75 mol O₂, while 0.906 mol O₂ is present); 1.50 mol (27.0 g) of water forms and 0.156 mol (5.0 g) of O₂ is left over
B) O₂ is limiting; 32.6 g of water forms and no reactant is left
C) H₂ is limiting; 13.5 g of water forms and 14.5 g of O₂ is left over
D) Neither is limiting; 32.0 g of water forms because mass is conserved
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) H₂ limiting; 27.0 g water; 5.0 g O₂ left.
Concept: Many a time, reactions are carried out with amounts of reactants that are different from the amounts required by a balanced chemical reaction; in such situations one reactant is in more amount than the amount required by the balanced reaction; the reactant which is present in the least amount gets consumed after some time, and after that no further reaction takes place whatever be the amount of the other reactant; hence, the reactant which gets consumed limits the amount of product formed and is therefore called the limiting reagent. To identify it, compare the mole ratio of the reactants available with that required by the balanced equation. Mass is conserved overall: the mass of product plus the unreacted reactant equals the total mass taken.
Given: m(H₂) = 3.0 g (M = 2), m(O₂) = 29.0 g (M = 32).
Formula/Principle: n = m/M; compare with stoichiometric ratio 2 : 1.
Step 1: n(H₂) = 1.50 mol; n(O₂) = 0.906 mol.
Step 2: 1.50 mol H₂ needs 0.75 mol O₂ < 0.906 ⇒ H₂ limiting.
Step 3: n(H₂O) = 1.50 mol = 27.0 g; O₂ left = 0.156 mol = 5.0 g.
Why: The reaction stops when the hydrogen runs out, and the leftover oxygen stays unreacted.
Why not the others: (B) O₂ is in excess. (C) Water mass halved. (D) 32 g is the total mass of water plus leftover O₂; one reactant is limiting.
Key point: Limiting reagent is decided by moles relative to the balanced equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Explaining trends in atomic radius, metallic character and oxide nature across p-block periods and down groups, including the anomalous radius of gallium
questions.question: Which statement about p-block trends is correct?
options: A) Gallium is larger than aluminium because size always increases down a group
B) Across a period the oxides become more basic, so Cl₂O₇ is the most basic oxide of period 3

C) Down group 13 the atomic radius rises from B to Al, but gallium (135 pm) is slightly smaller than aluminium (143 pm), because the ten 3d electrons in gallium shield poorly and its electrons feel a larger effective nuclear charge; across a period, non-metallic character increases and oxides change from basic (Na₂O) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (Cl₂O₇); down a group metallic character increases, and the stability of the lower oxidation state (ns² inert pair) increases in heavier elements
D) Metallic character decreases down a group in the p-block
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ga smaller than Al due to poor 3d shielding; oxides basic → amphoteric → acidic across a period; metallic character and inert pair effect increase down groups.
Concept: In the p-block, the atomic radius increases on moving down the group, as one more shell is added; however, a deviation can be seen: the atomic radius of Ga is less than that of Al; this can be understood from the variation in the inner core of the electronic configuration — the presence of an additional 10 d electrons offers only poor screening effect for the outer electrons from the increased nuclear charge in gallium; consequently, the atomic radius of gallium (135 pm) is less than that of aluminium (143 pm). Across a period, metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases; the elements on the extreme left form strongly basic oxides (e.g. Na₂O), whereas those on the extreme right form strongly acidic oxides (e.g. Cl₂O₇); oxides of elements in the centre are amphoteric (e.g. Al₂O₃, As₂O₃) or neutral (e.g. CO, NO, N₂O). Down a group in the p-block, metallic character increases; non-metals at the top give way to metalloids and then metals at the bottom. The occurrence of oxidation states two units less than the group oxidation states is sometimes attributed to the 'inert pair effect'; the relative stability of the lower oxidation state increases down the group (e.g. Tl⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺).
Why: Poorly shielding d electrons increase the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons of gallium, pulling them closer.
Why not the others: (A) Gallium is an exception. (B) Oxides become more acidic across a period. (D) Metallic character increases down a group.
Key point: r(Ga) < r(Al); oxides: basic → amphoteric → acidic across a period.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the C–O bond lengths in CO, CO₂ and CO₃²⁻ from their bond orders and resonance structures, and explaining resonance stabilisation
questions.question: Which ordering of C–O bond lengths, with reasoning, is correct?
options: A) CO₃²⁻ < CO₂ < CO, because more oxygen atoms shorten each bond

B) CO (triple bond, bond order 3, about 113 pm) < CO₂ (bond order 2, about 115 pm) < CO₃²⁻ (bond order 1⅓, about 129 pm); the carbonate ion cannot be described by one Lewis structure — it is a resonance hybrid of three equivalent structures, so all three C–O bonds are equal in length, intermediate between single and double; the hybrid is lower in energy than any single canonical structure, the difference being the resonance energy, and canonical forms have no real existence
C) All three have equal C–O bond lengths because carbon is always tetravalent
D) In CO₃²⁻ one bond is double and two are single, so there are two different bond lengths
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) CO < CO₂ < CO₃²⁻; carbonate is a resonance hybrid with equal bonds of order 1⅓.
Concept: Bond order is given by the number of bonds between the two atoms in a molecule; with increase in bond order, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases; in CO there is a triple bond (bond order 3), in CO₂ each C–O bond is a double bond (bond order 2). It is often observed that a single Lewis structure is inadequate for the representation of a molecule in conformity with its experimentally determined parameters; according to the concept of resonance, whenever a single Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule accurately, a number of structures with similar energy, positions of nuclei, bonding and non-bonding pairs of electrons are taken as the canonical structures of the hybrid which describes the molecule accurately; the carbonate ion is a resonance hybrid of three canonical forms; resonance stabilises the molecule, as the energy of the resonance hybrid is less than the energy of any single canonical structure; resonance averages the bond characteristics as a whole; the energy difference between the actual structure and the lowest-energy resonance structure is called the resonance stabilisation energy or simply the resonance energy; the canonical forms have no real existence, and the molecule does not exist for a certain fraction of time in one canonical form and for other fractions of time in other canonical forms. For the carbonate ion, bond order = total bonds/number of bonding positions = 4/3 ≈ 1.33.
Why: Bond length shortens as more electron pairs are shared between the atoms, and resonance spreads the double-bond character equally over the three carbonate bonds.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed. (C) Bond orders differ, so lengths differ. (D) Resonance makes all three bonds equal.
Key point: Higher bond order ⇒ shorter bond; resonance hybrids have averaged, equal bonds.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding circles that touch both coordinate axes and pass through a given point, and testing whether two circles touch externally or internally
questions.question: Find the radii of the circles in the first quadrant that touch both axes and pass through \((2,1)\). Do the circles \(x^2+y^2=4\) and \((x-6)^2+y^2=16\) touch, and if so where?
options: A) \(r=1\text{ or }5;\ \text{they touch externally at }(2,0)\)
B) \(r=2\text{ or }3;\ \text{they touch internally at }(-2,0)\)
C) \(r=5\text{ only};\ \text{they intersect at two points}\)
D) \(r=1\text{ or }5;\ \text{they do not meet}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(r=1\text{ or }5;\ \text{external contact at }(2,0)\)
Concept: \(\text{A circle touching both axes in the first quadrant has centre }(r,r)\text{ and radius }r;\ \text{two circles touch externally when the distance between centres equals the sum of the radii, internally when it equals their difference}\)
Given: \(\text{point }(2,1);\ C_1=(0,0),r_1=2;\ C_2=(6,0),r_2=4\)
Formula/Principle: \((x-r)^2+(y-r)^2=r^2;\ d=r_1+r_2\Rightarrow\text{external contact}\)
Step 1: \((2-r)^2+(1-r)^2=r^2\Rightarrow r^2-6r+5=0\)
Step 2: \((r-1)(r-5)=0\Rightarrow r=1\text{ or }5\)
Step 3: \(d=6=2+4\Rightarrow\text{external};\ \text{contact point divides }C_1C_2\text{ in }2:4\Rightarrow(2,0)\)
Worked derivation: \[(2-r)^2+(1-r)^2=r^2\Rightarrow4-4r+r^2+1-2r+r^2=r^2\Rightarrow r^2-6r+5=0\]
Check: \[r=5:\ (2-5)^2+(1-5)^2=9+16=25=5^2;\ \ (2,0)\text{ lies on both circles}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{touching both axes fixes the centre on }y=x\text{ at distance }r\text{ from each axis, leaving one unknown}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{radii do not satisfy the equation; }d\ne|r_1-r_2|\); (C) \(r=1\text{ also works; }d=r_1+r_2\text{ means one common point}\); (D) \(\text{the circles do meet at }(2,0)\).
Key point: \(\text{centre }(r,r);\ d=r_1+r_2\Rightarrow\text{external tangency}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Writing the equation of a circle from its centre and a point on it, and counting lattice points on a circle centred at the origin
questions.question: Find the equation of the circle with centre \((2,-3)\) passing through \((5,1)\), and the number of points with integer coordinates on \(x^2+y^2=25\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=25;\ 12\text{ lattice points}\)
Concept: \(\text{The circle with centre }(h,k)\text{ and radius }r\text{ is }(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2;\ \text{lattice points on }x^2+y^2=25\text{ come from integer solutions of }a^2+b^2=25\)
Given: \(\text{centre }(2,-3),\ \text{point }(5,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(r^2=(5-2)^2+(1+3)^2\)
Step 1: \(r^2=9+16=25\)
Step 2: \((x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=25\Rightarrow x^2+y^2-4x+6y+13-25=0\)
Step 3: \(25=0^2+5^2=3^2+4^2\Rightarrow(\pm5,0),(0,\pm5)\ [4],\ (\pm3,\pm4),(\pm4,\pm3)\ [8]\Rightarrow12\)
Worked derivation: \[x^2-4x+4+y^2+6y+9=25\Rightarrow x^2+y^2-4x+6y-12=0\]
Check: \[(5,1):\ 25+1-20+6-12=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the radius is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{used }r\text{ instead of }r^2\); (B) \(\text{signs of the centre wrong; misses }(\pm3,\pm4)\text{ type points}\); (C) \(\text{constant term wrong}\).
Key point: \((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Computing conditional probabilities from given probabilities and in special cases where one event contains the other or the events are mutually exclusive
questions.question: If \(P(A)=0.6,\ P(B)=0.3,\ P(A\cap B)=0.2\), find \(P(A\mid B)\) and \(P(B\mid A)\). What is \(P(A\mid B)\) if \(B\subset A\), and if \(A,B\) are mutually exclusive with \(P(B)>0\)? A die is rolled; given that the number is odd, what is the probability it is prime?
options: A) \(\tfrac12,\ \tfrac12;\ 0;\ 1;\ \tfrac12\)
B) \(\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23;\ P(A);\ P(B);\ \tfrac13\)
C) \(\tfrac23,\ \tfrac13;\ 1;\ 0;\ \tfrac23\)
D) \(\tfrac23,\ \tfrac13;\ 0;\ 1;\ \tfrac13\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\tfrac23,\ \tfrac13;\ 1;\ 0;\ \tfrac23\)
Concept: \(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\ P(B)\ne0;\ \text{it is the probability of }A\text{ when the sample space is reduced to }B\)
Given: \(P(A)=0.6,\ P(B)=0.3,\ P(A\cap B)=0.2\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\)
Step 1: \(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.3}=\tfrac23;\ P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.6}=\tfrac13\)
Step 2: \(B\subset A\Rightarrow A\cap B=B\Rightarrow P(A\mid B)=1;\ A\cap B=\varnothing\Rightarrow P(A\mid B)=0\)
Step 3: \(\text{odd}=\{1,3,5\},\ \text{odd and prime}=\{3,5\}\Rightarrow\tfrac23\)
Worked derivation: \[P(\text{prime}\mid\text{odd})=\frac{P(\{3,5\})}{P(\{1,3,5\})}=\frac{2/6}{3/6}=\frac23\]
Check: \[P(A\mid B)P(B)=\tfrac23\cdot0.3=0.2=P(B\mid A)P(A)=\tfrac13\cdot0.6\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{conditioning restricts attention to outcomes inside }B,\ \text{so containment gives certainty and disjointness gives impossibility}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{values and special cases wrong}\); (B) \(\text{the two conditionals are swapped}\); (D) \(\text{special cases reversed; die answer wrong}\).
Key point: \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reading the graphs of inverse sine and inverse cosine to find where they intersect and where one exceeds the other, and using their domains and ranges
questions.question: On \([-1,1]\), the graphs of \(y=\sin^{-1}x\) and \(y=\cos^{-1}x\) are drawn. At which point do they intersect, for which \(x\) is \(\sin^{-1}x>\cos^{-1}x\), and what is \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x\) for every \(x\in[-1,1]\)?
options: B) \(\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right);\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2}<x\le1;\ \tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
C) \(\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right);\ x>\tfrac12;\ \tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
D) \(\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right);\ -1\le x<\tfrac1{\sqrt2};\ 0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right);\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2}<x\le1;\ \tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Concept: \(y=\sin^{-1}x\text{ increases from }(-1,-\tfrac{\pi}{2})\text{ to }(1,\tfrac{\pi}{2});\ y=\cos^{-1}x\text{ decreases from }(-1,\pi)\text{ to }(1,0);\ \text{their sum is }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Given: \(\text{both graphs on }[-1,1]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\text{intersection}\Rightarrow\sin^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow x=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)
Step 2: \(\sin^{-1}x>\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin^{-1}x\iff\sin^{-1}x>\tfrac{\pi}{4}\iff x>\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\)
Step 3: \(\text{increasing}+\text{decreasing curves cross once; sum constant}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\theta=\sin^{-1}x\Rightarrow x=\sin\theta=\cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right),\ \tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\in[0,\pi]\Rightarrow\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\]
Check: \[x=1:\ \sin^{-1}1=\tfrac{\pi}{2}>\cos^{-1}1=0;\ \ x=0:\ 0<\tfrac{\pi}{2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the two graphs are reflections of each other about the line }y=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{at }x=0\text{ the values are }0\text{ and }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\); (C) \(\cos^{-1}\tfrac12=\tfrac{\pi}{3}\ne\tfrac{\pi}{6}\); (D) \(\text{inequality reversed; sum is not 0}\).
Key point: \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a system of three linear equations by the matrix inverse method after checking that the coefficient matrix is non-singular
questions.question: Solve \(x+y+z=6,\ x-y+z=2,\ 2x+y-z=1\) by the matrix method. What is \(|A|\) for the coefficient matrix, and what is the solution?
options: A) \(|A|=0;\ \text{infinitely many solutions}\)
D) \(|A|=6\ne0,\ \text{so }A^{-1}\text{ exists and the unique solution is }X=A^{-1}B=(1,2,3)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(|A|=6;\ (x,y,z)=(1,2,3)\)
Concept: \(\text{For }AX=B,\ \text{if }|A|\ne0\text{ then }A\text{ is invertible and }X=A^{-1}B=\dfrac{1}{|A|}(\operatorname{adj}A)B\text{ is the unique solution}\)
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&-1&1\\2&1&-1\end{pmatrix},\ B=\begin{pmatrix}6\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(X=A^{-1}B\)
Step 1: \(|A|=1(1-1)-1(-1-2)+1(1+2)=0+3+3=6\)
Step 2: \(\text{eq1}-\text{eq2}:\ 2y=4\Rightarrow y=2;\ \text{then }x+z=4,\ 2x-z=-1\)
Step 3: \(3x=3\Rightarrow x=1,\ z=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&2\\3&-3&0\\3&1&-2\end{pmatrix},\ \ A^{-1}B=\frac16\begin{pmatrix}0+4+2\\18-6+0\\18+2-2\end{pmatrix}=\frac16\begin{pmatrix}6\\12\\18\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\]
Check: \[1+2+3=6,\ 1-2+3=2,\ 2+2-3=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a non-zero determinant guarantees exactly one solution, which the inverse delivers}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|A|\ne0\); (B) \(\text{sign of }|A|\text{ and the solution wrong}\); (C) \((2,1,3)\text{ fails the second equation}\).
Key point: \(|A|\ne0\Rightarrow X=A^{-1}B\text{ unique}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the parameters that make a piecewise function continuous and differentiable at the joining point, and a function that is continuous but not differentiable
questions.question: \(f(x)=x^2\) for \(x\le1\) and \(f(x)=ax+b\) for \(x>1\). Find \(a,b\) so that \(f\) is differentiable at \(x=1\). Which of \(|x|\) and \(x|x|\) is differentiable at \(x=0\)?
options: A) \(a=2,\ b=-1;\ x|x|\text{ is differentiable at 0, }|x|\text{ is not}\)
B) \(a=1,\ b=0;\ \text{both are differentiable}\)
C) \(a=2,\ b=1;\ |x|\text{ is differentiable, }x|x|\text{ is not}\)
D) \(a=-1,\ b=2;\ \text{neither is continuous at 0}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a=2,\ b=-1;\ x|x|\text{ differentiable at 0},\ |x|\text{ not}\)
Concept: \(\text{Differentiability at a point implies continuity there; the converse is false. At a joining point both the values and the one-sided derivatives must match}\)
Given: \(f=x^2\ (x\le1),\ ax+b\ (x>1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(f(1^-)=f(1^+);\ Lf'(1)=Rf'(1)\)
Step 1: \(\text{continuity: }1=a+b\)
Step 2: \(\text{derivatives: }2x\big|_{1}=2=a\Rightarrow b=-1\)
Step 3: \(|x|:\ Lf'(0)=-1,\ Rf'(0)=1\Rightarrow\text{not differentiable};\ x|x|:\ \lim_{h\to0}\tfrac{h|h|}{h}=0\Rightarrow\text{differentiable}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dx}(x|x|)\Big|_{0}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{h|h|-0}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}|h|=0\]
Check: \[x>1:\ f=2x-1,\ f(1^+)=1=f(1),\ f'=2=2(1)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{matching values removes a jump, and matching slopes removes a corner}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{slope 1 does not match }2x\text{ at }1\); (C) \(a+b=3\ne1;\ |x|\text{ has a corner}\); (D) \(\text{both are continuous at 0}\).
Key point: \(\text{differentiable}\Rightarrow\text{continuous, not conversely}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting the local maxima and minima of a quartic using the first and second derivative tests, and recognising a stationary point that is neither
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^4-8x^2\), how many points of local maximum and local minimum are there, and what are the extreme values? Is \(x=0\) a local extremum of \(g(x)=x^3\)?
options: A) \(2\text{ maxima, 1 minimum};\ \text{max }16;\ g\text{ has a minimum at 0}\)
B) \(1\text{ maximum, 1 minimum};\ \text{min }-8;\ g\text{ has a maximum at 0}\)
C) \(1\text{ local maximum (at }x=0,\ f=0)\text{ and 2 local minima (at }x=\pm2,\ f=-16);\ x=0\text{ is a point of inflexion of }g,\ \text{not an extremum}\)
D) \(0\text{ maxima, 3 minima};\ g\text{ has a minimum at 0}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\text{max at }0\ (f=0);\ \text{minima at }\pm2\ (f=-16);\ g\text{ has an inflexion at }0\)
Concept: \(\text{If }f'(c)=0\text{ and }f''(c)<0,\ c\text{ is a local maximum; if }f''(c)>0,\ \text{a local minimum; if }f'\text{ does not change sign at }c,\ c\text{ is neither (a point of inflexion)}\)
Given: \(f=x^4-8x^2;\ g=x^3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{second derivative test}\)
Step 1: \(f'=4x^3-16x=4x(x-2)(x+2)=0\Rightarrow x=0,\pm2\)
Step 2: \(f''=12x^2-16:\ f''(0)=-16<0\ (\max),\ f''(\pm2)=32>0\ (\min)\)
Step 3: \(f(0)=0,\ f(\pm2)=16-32=-16;\ g'=3x^2\ge0\text{ never changes sign}\Rightarrow\text{no extremum}\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(x)=4x(x^2-4):\ \ x<-2:\ -;\ \ -2<x<0:\ +;\ \ 0<x<2:\ -;\ \ x>2:\ +\]
Check: \[f(1)=1-8=-7<0=f(0)\text{ and }f(3)=81-72=9>-16=f(2)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{sign changes of }f'\text{ from }+\text{ to }-\text{ mark maxima and from }-\text{ to }+\text{ mark minima}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts reversed}\); (B) \(\text{misses the second minimum; value wrong}\); (D) \(x=0\text{ is a maximum of }f;\ g\text{ has no extremum}\).
Key point: \(f''<0\Rightarrow\max,\ f''>0\Rightarrow\min;\ f'\text{ without sign change}\Rightarrow\text{inflexion}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating indefinite integrals by choosing a suitable substitution in rational, exponential and logarithmic integrands
questions.question: Evaluate \(I_1=\displaystyle\int\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\,dx\), \(I_2=\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^2}\,dx\) and \(I_3=\displaystyle\int\frac{(\ln x)^2}{x}\,dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\ln(1+x^2)+C,\ e^{\tan^{-1}x}+C,\ \tfrac13(\ln x)^3+C\)
Concept: \(\text{If the integrand contains a function }g(x)\text{ together with }g'(x),\ \text{put }t=g(x),\ dt=g'(x)\,dx\text{ to reduce it to a standard form}\)
Given: \(\text{the three integrands}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=\int f(t)\,dt\)
Step 1: \(t=1+x^2,\ dt=2x\,dx\Rightarrow\int\tfrac{dt}{t}=\ln(1+x^2)+C\)
Step 2: \(t=\tan^{-1}x,\ dt=\tfrac{dx}{1+x^2}\Rightarrow\int e^t\,dt=e^{\tan^{-1}x}+C\)
Step 3: \(t=\ln x,\ dt=\tfrac{dx}{x}\Rightarrow\int t^2\,dt=\tfrac13(\ln x)^3+C\)
Worked derivation: \[\int\frac{(\ln x)^2}{x}dx\ \overset{t=\ln x}{=}\ \int t^2\,dt=\frac{t^3}{3}+C=\frac{(\ln x)^3}{3}+C\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[\tfrac13(\ln x)^3\right]=(\ln x)^2\cdot\frac1x\ \checkmark;\ \ \frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each integrand is a function of }g(x)\text{ multiplied by }g'(x),\ \text{the signal for substitution}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{derivatives of these do not match the integrands}\); (C) \(\text{wrong antiderivatives}\); (D) \(\text{extra factor 2 in }I_1;\ \text{wrong power in }I_3\).
Key point: \(\text{spot }g\text{ and }g'\text{ together}\Rightarrow t=g(x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating rational functions by partial fractions and interpreting a definite integral of a positive rational function as an area
questions.question: Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}\), the area under \(y=\dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x-2)}\) from \(x=3\) to \(x=4\), and \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x+1)(x+2)}\).
options: B) \(\ln\left|\tfrac{x-1}{x-2}\right|+C;\ \ln\tfrac34;\ 2\ln|x+1|-\ln|x+2|+C\)
D) \(\ln\left|\tfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|+C;\ \ln\tfrac43;\ 2\ln|x+2|-\ln|x+1|+C\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\ln\left|\tfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|+C;\ \ln\tfrac43;\ 2\ln|x+2|-\ln|x+1|+C\)
Concept: \(\text{A proper rational function with distinct linear factors in the denominator splits as }\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{B}{x-b};\ \text{for a positive integrand, the definite integral is the area under the curve}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x-2)},\ \dfrac{x}{(x+1)(x+2)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\dfrac{1}{x-2}-\dfrac{1}{x-1}\)
Step 1: \(\int=\ln|x-2|-\ln|x-1|=\ln\left|\tfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|+C\)
Step 2: \(\text{area}=\left[\ln\tfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right]_3^4=\ln\tfrac23-\ln\tfrac12=\ln\tfrac43\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{x}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\dfrac{-1}{x+1}+\dfrac{2}{x+2}\Rightarrow2\ln|x+2|-\ln|x+1|+C\)
Worked derivation: \[x=A(x+2)+B(x+1):\ x=-1\Rightarrow A=-1;\ x=-2\Rightarrow B=2\]
Check: \[\text{on }[3,4],\ y>0\text{ and }\ln\tfrac43\approx0.288,\ \text{between }y(4)\cdot1=\tfrac16\text{ and }y(3)\cdot1=\tfrac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{splitting into simple fractions turns the integrand into terms whose integrals are logarithms}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{coefficients are not both }+1\); (B) \(\text{sign reversed, giving a negative area}\); (C) \(\text{partial fractions integrate to logs, not reciprocals}\).
Key point: \(\text{distinct linear factors}\Rightarrow\sum\dfrac{A_i}{x-a_i}\Rightarrow\text{logarithms}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the projection of one vector on another, the angle between them, and the value of a parameter that makes two vectors perpendicular
questions.question: For \(\vec a=2\hat i+3\hat j+6\hat k\) and \(\vec b=\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k\), find the projection of \(\vec b\) on \(\vec a\), \(\cos\theta\), and the value of \(\lambda\) for which \(\vec a\perp(\hat i+\lambda\hat j+\hat k)\).
options: A) \(\tfrac{20}{7};\ \tfrac{20}{21};\ \lambda=-\tfrac83\)
B) \(\tfrac{20}{3};\ \tfrac{20}{21};\ \lambda=\tfrac83\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\tfrac{20}{7};\ \tfrac{20}{21};\ \lambda=-\tfrac83\)
Concept: \(\text{Projection of }\vec b\text{ on }\vec a=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a|};\ \cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a||\vec b|};\ \vec a\perp\vec c\iff\vec a\cdot\vec c=0\)
Given: \(\vec a=(2,3,6),\ \vec b=(1,2,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\)
Step 1: \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=2+6+12=20;\ |\vec a|=7,\ |\vec b|=3\)
Step 2: \(\text{projection}=\tfrac{20}{7};\ \cos\theta=\tfrac{20}{21}\)
Step 3: \(2+3\lambda+6=0\Rightarrow\lambda=-\tfrac83\)
Worked derivation: \[|\vec a|=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7,\ \ |\vec b|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3,\ \ \cos\theta=\frac{20}{7\cdot3}\]
Check: \[\text{projection}=|\vec b|\cos\theta=3\cdot\tfrac{20}{21}=\tfrac{20}{7}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the dot product measures how much of one vector lies along the other}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{divided by }|\vec b|;\ \text{sign of }\lambda\text{ wrong}\); (C) \(\text{not normalised}\); (D) \(\cos\theta\text{ inverted; }\lambda=0\text{ gives }8\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{proj}_{\vec a}\vec b=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Writing the vector and Cartesian equations of a line through a point parallel to a vector, and the special case of a line parallel to a coordinate axis
questions.question: Find the Cartesian equation of the line through \((1,2,3)\) parallel to \(3\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k\), its direction cosines, and the equations of the line through \((1,2,3)\) parallel to the \(z\)-axis.
options: A) \(\dfrac{x-3}{1}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z+2}{3};\ \left(\tfrac37,\tfrac27,-\tfrac27\right);\ z=3\)
B) \(\dfrac{x-1}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z-3}{-2};\ \left(\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{17}},\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{17}},-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{17}}\right);\ x=1,\ y=2\ (z\text{ free})\)
D) \(\dfrac{x-1}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z-3}{2};\ \left(\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{17}},\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{17}},\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{17}}\right);\ x=1,\ z=3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{x-1}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z-3}{-2};\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}(3,2,-2);\ x=1,\ y=2\)
Concept: \(\text{The line through }\vec a\text{ parallel to }\vec b\text{ is }\vec r=\vec a+\lambda\vec b;\ \text{in Cartesian form }\dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c};\ \text{a line parallel to the }z\text{-axis has d.r. }(0,0,1)\)
Given: \(\text{point }(1,2,3),\ \vec b=(3,2,-2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{d.c.}=\dfrac{(a,b,c)}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{x-1}{3}=\dfrac{y-2}{2}=\dfrac{z-3}{-2}\)
Step 2: \(|\vec b|=\sqrt{9+4+4}=\sqrt{17}\Rightarrow\text{d.c.}=\left(\tfrac3{\sqrt{17}},\tfrac2{\sqrt{17}},-\tfrac2{\sqrt{17}}\right)\)
Step 3: \(\text{d.r. }(0,0,1)\Rightarrow x-1=0,\ y-2=0\)
